title: Sony WF-C510 Truly Wireless Bluetooth Earbud Headphones, Black
description: ALL DAY COMFORT: Light and compact to give you all-day comfort and designed for the ideal fit, for an exceptional all-round listening experience. MULTIPOINT CONNECTION: Quickly switch between two devices at once. STAY CONNECTED: Ambient Sound Mode keeps you aware of your surroundings. reviews: [{"review_id": "R1P23JTET1LCL1", "reviewer_name": "The Matt", "headline": "Sony WF-C510 -- Good Audio For Cheap", "review_text": "1) The sound of the WF-C510 is really good right out of the box without EQ. I listen to a lot of music, various genres, and everything is balanced and in control. Punchy bass, treble that's crisp and doesn't make my ears bleed, and decent mids. I definitely trust Sony when it comes to audio products. 2) Fit and comfort are amazing! I can leave these in all day. No joke, after 5+ hours of use, I feel zero discomfort. Not only are these earbuds the most comfortable earbuds of all time, but getting a good in-ear seal is effortless. Just set them and forget them, zero hassle. Just to note, there's no ANC but I don't mind; I use these at home where it's already quiet. Further, there's a feature called Ambient Sound Control, kind of the opposite of ANC, that lets outside noises in (press button on left earbud). Obviously, the volume has to be pretty low for this feature to be useful. 3) I rarely ever use playback controls on a pair of earbuds, as I just use my phone for that stuff. However, the physical buttons on the WF-C510 work like they should and it's always nice to have actual buttons over touch controls, mainly because there's less chance for accidental inputs, a common occurrence on my other earbuds. 4) The battery life seems to jive with Sony's claims of 11 hours in the buds and another 11 in the case. I'm getting a 50% battery level after 5+ hours at a volume level above half with the \"Sony Sound Connect\" app installed on my phone. I'll admit, the 11 hour battery claim was the #1 factor for my purchase. 5) The app gives you a ton of stuff to play around with. There's a bunch of EQs, 360 audio (more app downloads and payment required, I think), information regarding battery levels, and more. 6) A couple of oddities: The charging case confuses me. Does the orange light turn off when charging is complete or does it stay lit? I've experienced both scenarios and both times the app said the earbuds and case were at 100%. The instruction manual was no help. Also, for some reason I had to re-pair the earbuds to my phone's Bluetooth after shutting it off, which was super annoying. I was testing to see if an older device (without the app) would pair, so to avoid interference I turned off my phone's Bluetooth. The older device paired with the earbuds just fine without the app, so it isn't required. I plan on deleting it; it's probably a major battery hog anyway. 7) Minor issues aside, the Sony WF-C510 delivers premium comfort and pleasing sound. and they're super affordable. Get yours today! lol Update 3/25 -- Checking in to mention that the orange charging light on the case does in fact shut off to indicate that charging is complete and I'm still very happy with my purchase.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on December 30, 2024"}, {"review_id": "RRIY5JP04P6O6", "reviewer_name": "GraniteStateColin", "headline": "Physical buttons + Water resistance = works in heavy rain and shower (unlike ALL capacitive earbuds)", "review_text": "I don't understand the logic behind other earbuds that claim water resistance with capacitive controls. I have tried almost a dozen across various brands and NONE of them work properly when wet. It's not that the water damages them (it doesn't), it's that the capacitive buttons can't tell a water drop from a finger, so they're constantly registering false touches, jumping tracks, changing volume. CAPACITIVE EARBUDS ARE USELESS WHEN WET. (Fine once they dry off.) This WF-C510 pair from Sony, with physical buttons instead of capacitive touch, is the FIRST SET EARBUDS I'VE FOUND THAT ACTULLY WORK IN THE SHOWER or heavy rain. If you're just going for a jog in light mist or some drops of sweat run down your ears, those others do OK, but in a heavy rain or if you want to listen in the shower, go for these. I use earbuds in the shower so I don't wake up my spouse or kids if I get up early. I used to use a suction cup Bluetooth speaker, but that's loud and disturbs the family. Another problem with many capacitive earbuds: if you don't have any audio playing for a few minutes, they'll turn off to save battery... but because the capacitive touch requires power to work, there's often no way to turn them back on without putting them in the case and then removing them. This means if you don't have the case with you, you can't use them at all. I have actually bought extra cases just to leave in the places I often get stuck with powered-off earbuds, but what a waste of money that is! But note that where JBL, for example, sells just extra cases for their capacitive buds, I don't see that Sony does that. While you don't really need an extra case for these because you can turn them on and off via buttons, in the event you do want an extra case, be aware that your only option might be used on eBay. Also, these Sony WFD-C510 earbuds are small (compact, in the best possible way). These are some of the few earbuds I've found that I can wear under ear protection when mowing or doing other loud equipment work. Most other earbuds are bulky in comparison and ear protection pushes against them directly, really digging into the ear. These are so slim, you barely feel them even while wearing ear protection over them. On sound quality, these are great. They're not the best overall, but I think they are the best per dollar (and no earbuds are as good as real headphones if sound quality is the primary goal). They sound amazing for $50 buds. So, yes, overall, I would highly recommend them to anyone, but especially if you care about using them when very wet or under ear protection. Best I've found for those scenarios by a wide margin. To address both issues with a single pair of earbuds is incredible. One of my favorite bits of tech ever.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on July 24, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R2ND1P8ZN3SMRG", "reviewer_name": "Carter Davis", "headline": "amazing value", "review_text": "Bought these to replace my favorite earbuds of the past few years, the KZ SKS and was a little disappointed at first. That was until I tweaked the EQ in the SONY app, which these responded wonderfully to. The bass is very lacking out of the box, but it makes for balanced tone. I like a lot of bass and bright highs, so I moved the slider to 7 on bass and adjusted the others accordingly, with no loss in sound quality. The biggest change though, was the exceptional battery life and amazing passthrough mode that I did not expect to like as much as I do. It allows conversations to be carried out while on the phone or listening to music. Even though these are roughly double the price of my $30 KZs, I would actually say they're an even better value with the features and battery life. They're also super light and relatively small, so they won't fall out of your ears. For a 6mm driver (which is supposedly shared with some of their more expensive models), these have an excellent soundstage and really can thump. The ONLY drawback (if you want to call it that), is the buttons are not capacitive, and must be physically clicked. This can be helpful in preventing accidental presses though, which is a plus. Build quality is what you'd expect from Sony. Very good. Will update if these have any drawbacks in the future.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on February 22, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R1UFYD9AKIQWOA", "reviewer_name": "Freddy Cruz", "headline": "Good Value for the Price, with Some Clear Limitations", "review_text": "I purchased the Sony WF-C510 for around $50 or less, and considering that price point, I am generally satisfied with the product. Below is my experience after a few weeks of use. Sound: For the price, the sound profile is good and well balanced. The bass is present, though not very powerful compared to more expensive models. As a user who has owned higher-end earbuds, I do notice a lack of depth in the low frequencies, but at this price range, that is acceptable. You cannot expect premium bass performance from a budget model, and within those limits, the sound is decent. Comfort: The earbuds are small and lightweight, and after some time you barely notice you are wearing them. They are comfortable enough to use while lying in bed, and if they had touch controls, you could even listen while resting on one side without discomfort. That said, the fit is not perfect for me. They do not feel 100% secure at all times, and I occasionally need to readjust them manually. It is not frequent, but it is an area that could be improved. Buttons: For the price, I did not expect touch controls, but the physical buttons can be inconvenient at times. Pressing them often causes the earbud to move out of position, which then requires readjustment. Microphone: Based on feedback from my wife during phone calls, there was noticeable background noise on my end. I cannot provide a very detailed review of the microphone, but this was the main comment I received during the three weeks of use. Would I recommend them? It depends on the use case. I would not recommend them for intense workouts. If you are very demanding about sound quality or expect a high-end audio profile, these will likely disappoint you. However, for walking, office use, or casual listening—and if you are not very demanding about sound quality—they are a good option for the price. Note: I have used the Jabra Elite 75t for about two years (originally $199) and have been using the Sony WH-1000XM3 for four years. Obviously, this is not a fair comparison, as the difference in sound quality is significant. Still, considering the price of the WF-C510, they are worth it if you are not overly demanding about audio performance. ============================ Update after a few months of use: ============================ After a couple of months with the Sony WF-C510, my overall opinion remains mostly the same, but I can now add a few clearer conclusions. The biggest downside is definitely the microphone. Call quality has consistently been poor. On several occasions during meetings, I had to disconnect them and switch to other headphones to continue the call. Background noise isolation for the mic is weak, and for professional use, they are simply not reliable. The sound profile is still good for the price. It remains balanced and acceptable within its budget category. However, if you are used to earbuds in the $150+ range, these will likely feel underpowered and lacking depth. The difference in presence, clarity, and overall audio richness becomes more noticeable over time. Would I buy them again? Probably not. While they are not bad for the price, I personally prefer stronger audio performance and more depth, even if that means paying more. Overall, my experience is neutral — not bad, not exceptional. They deliver what you would expect from a $48 pair of earbuds, but they do not meet my personal expectations, which are influenced by years of using higher-end models.", "rating": "4.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on December 31, 2025"}, {"review_id": "R2P9GG8C0PQVLC", "reviewer_name": "Scott's Reviews", "headline": "Exceptionally good, amazing even, 'buds at a great price", "review_text": "These are amazing. The sound quality is very good. They don't fall out of my ears (all other earbuds i've had, lots of them, don't stay in my ears. Even my AirPods Pro 2 fall out of my ears, but not these. Although they lack noise cancelation, they do significantly reduce environmental noise. The buds form a tight seal, and turning off the Ambient Noise feature makes them effectively noise canceling. BUT, the most impressive feature is the water resistance. I, ummmmmmm, left them in my pants pocket, forgot they were there, and put the pants in the washing machine. Yeah, very much bad not good. That night I put them in a UV dryer and cycled it several times. The next morning I tested them AND THEY WORKED. Holy Moly Batman! These are tough buds.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on June 25, 2026"}, {"review_id": "RTVMB4DPL2BE8", "reviewer_name": "Erin S.", "headline": "Great Audio, Great Fit, One Big Problem", "review_text": "I purchased these a little under a year ago, and up until about a month ago, I absolutely loved them. title: Soundcore P30i by Anker Noise Cancelling Earbuds, Hands-Free Viewing
description: 2-in-1 Charging Case and Phone Stand: Enjoy hands-free viewing without the hassle. Simply open the back panel of the case, place your phone on the stand, and catch up on your favorite shows—watching while traveling has never been easier! Strong and Smart Noise Cancelling: Reduce noise by up to 42dB with an advanced active noise cancelling system. Transparency Mode: Let in the world or focus on your audio, the choice is yours. Simply switch to transparency mode to hear the world around you when needed. reviews: [{"review_id": "R1DYGKK8UFRC12", "reviewer_name": "Lee T.", "headline": "Very good sound for small price. Budget bangers!", "review_text": "Anker Soundcore P30i buds. First and foremost I want to be clear that I am rating these buds purely on their own merit. Without their software, without any Equalizer, just on how they perform straight out of the box. Baseus and Tozo and Jlabs are some of the names when we think of Budget Bass Buds. And for those who are looking for good, clean bass... I'd compare these with Jlabs. For bass, right out of the box, playing music with bass in it, they deliver a clear, audible thump, without the actual pounding vibration. Right now, I'm listening to Cry Little Sister, from the Lost Boys soundtrack, at volume EIGHT. (That's not even halfway up my volume bar from my phone). And the base tune soundstage is really, really good. Especially for a bass tuned base. The vocals, and background vocals are right up front. Crisp, clear, and don't sound like they are being overwhelmed by anything. And I can definitely hear every hit from the bass drums, as well as count the cords on the keyboard. Now I'm at 12, and those bass drums are starting to pound. Other than it's significantly louder, I'm still hearing good clarity of the different ranges. I can't say this for my Tozo T18 Crystal buds, without tuning. My Baseus BP1 pros would be creeping over the midrange at this volume on the base tune. Ok, now I'm at 18. A lot louder than I usually listen to. The highs are much more prominent over the lows. Which is the opposite of how a lot of bass speakers work. Honestly, this kind of division of the ranges from a single driver speaker is kind of surprising, especially at 20 to 25 dollars. Battery life is good too. I have a 10 hour day. 2 hours on the bus, 8 hour shift at work. With the ANC turned on, they need a quick charge at lunch to carry me home. With ANC turned off, yeah, I can get back in the door before they need to be charged. Sometimes just barely, if I've had them cranked up. ANC- on the bus they do pretty good. Cuts down a lot of the engine and sound noise from the bus. I can still hear people talking next to me, but at about half what it would be without the buds in. At work? Well it's so noisy at work even full blown ear muffs aren't making it good. Feel- ok this is subjective, because my right ear canal is different from my left. In my right, I can feel a bit of pressure when I put them in. But once in, they're quite comfortable, and I can fall asleep with them in, as a side-sleeper. Bluetooth is good. Stays connected as long as I'm in range, and range is definitely acceptable. Definitely better than the chap 17 dollar Onn buds I have. Easy to pair also. My only real complaint is no front panel to show the charge on the batteries. All said the bass isn't as deep on the base soundstage as Tozo delivers, but it's cleaner. Tozo also offers much better options in their software, as does Baseus, in some ways. I DO like a lot that SoundCore went the route of making the stems wider, instead of longer. Having long hair, it's less likely to get caught on the stems, and pull them out. Speaking of pulling them out. I decided to do some headbanging. My glasses flew off but these buds didn't budge. Overall though I have no regrets at all, buying these very good sounding set of inexpensive buds.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on October 25, 2025"}, {"review_id": "RE9UKEXG9J2QK", "reviewer_name": "Alexandre Sandor", "headline": "Shockingly satisfying in every possible way", "review_text": "After spending $1000 in headphones/earbuds in the last 3 years (1 Sony $390, 1 Samsung $350, 1 Google $199), and being disappointed with \"cost/benefit\" on all 3, I decided to give a shot at this absolutely inexpensive option. But before pressing \"buy now\" and just purchase it, I decided to do very same work I did when buying the other 3 premium devices, and took my time, reading reviews, educating myself about the company and it's commitment with customers/users, and finally, I went deep into the specs of the hardware, software, and the mobile app (this last one definitely a big plus). At this point you might say: \"it's a freaking $30 Bluetooth earbud\" just buy, use it, and if doesn't deliver it's promises, then just return it and add another \"zero\" to the original $30 and buy a premium device. Well, not so fast... I was intrigued by how good it all sounded and I want to use this whole experience to test an assumption I've been carrying for a short while, which is that we've been all scammed and abused with the so called premium priced devices, in other words , if you want the goods, you have to pay much higher price for it. So, I looked into this as an opportunity to unmask my theory and for that I had to put the \"works\" in place. After blending and filtering all the information gathered (the process even included \"unclutter suspicious\" reviews), the conclusion was obvious: despite all looking very standard, there was a positively intriguing desire to give it a try, and the result couldn't be more satisfying. Design looks average initially, but it actually reflects a distinct personality with a touch of elegance, specially with the colors available (green was my option and I was not disappointed). The hardware is absolutely underestimated for the price tag, meaning, it has the ability to deliver a sound quality that matches my Sony WH1000 (I listen to audio-music/books/podcasts an average of 6 hours a day) with crystal clear sound nuances, including a sharp treble and a solid bass, and yesssss, a battery life that will get you listening music and talking on the phone for a few days just by a one full charge on the charging case. Call quality... isn't this feature one of the most important components that will drive us towards or far away from a device...Yes!!!! So here it is: Shockingly amazing call quality. They built this right, and the balance between the software and the hardware, is in perfect harmony, 4 mics and AI, cleaning all the \"distractions\" away from phone conversations, and music listening without any disappointment. And here is the \"cherry in the cake: THE MOBILE APP. Again, another well built component of the whole experience. Better than my Sony, Google, and yes, heartbreaking, my Samsung (I'm a big fan of Samsung products). Summarizing, it's not Bluetooth 6.0, not 14mm sound shell, but it's absolutely a shocker of a quality device that only cost me $30, and it gives me peace of mind with call and music-sound quality. Noise Canceling absolutely under your control, through an app designed with everything you need to make it \"your way\", and satisfy your desire to listen music like a music producer ;) Ps: no one paid me to write this review, and despite the fact that I don't ever right a review, here is one I hope it will add value to your decision.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on June 5, 2025"}, {"review_id": "R370HA0Y2VCQ4N", "reviewer_name": "Pedro Senhorinha Silva II", "headline": "I’ve Never Had Earbuds Like This", "review_text": "I’ve bought a lot of headphones. And I can definitively say that the noise cancellation is better than any earbuds I’ve ever used. And then there’s the app. I’ve actually never had any earbuds with an app like this. These are so good in combination with the app that I hope they last for years and years to come.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 18, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R4U9Q2T0LI88R", "reviewer_name": "CA Consulting", "headline": "Exceptional sound and a comfortable fit at a great price", "review_text": "The title says it all. I have about 7 different earbuds and 5 over ear headphones varying in quality from okay to really good. This pair ranks up among my best. Balancing between comfort and sound quality these would be a good value at $50, at under 30 they were exceptional. title: Razer Viper V3 Pro Wireless Esports Gaming Mouse, 54g Lightweight, Black
description: 54 G ULTRA LIGHTWEIGHT DESIGN — Designed in collaboration with world-class esports pros, the Viper V3 Pro’s perfectly balanced ultra lightweight design allows gamers to make swift, precise flicks that match every intention FOCUS PRO 35K OPTICAL SENSOR GEN-2 — Experience pro grade tracking performance on a wider variety of surfaces including glass, supported by intelligent functions and 1-DPI step adjustments for more granular aim and control 8000 Hz HYPERPOLLING TECHNOLOGY — By combining Razer HyperPolling with the ultra smooth connection of Razer HyperSpeed, experience flawless wireless performance with a true polling rate of up to 8000 Hz HYPERSPEED WIRELESS — With an optimized dongle design that makes zero compromises on connection, enjoy top-tier wireless performance that remains smooth and reliable even in noisy tournament environments OPTICAL MOUSE SWITCHES GEN-3 — From an improved 90 million click lifecycle with zero double-clicking issues, to a blistering 0.2 ms actuation with no debounce delay, enjoy reliability and speed that outshines all others UP TO 95 HOURS OF BATTERY LIFE — Power through the most intense scrimming and tournament schedule with up to 95 hours of high-performance competitive gameplay OPTIMIZE MOUSE ACCURACY — Improve accuracy by disabling the "Enhance pointer precision" option in the Windows mouse settings, and further optimize performance using the Razer Synapse App
reviews: [{"review_id": "R2YUBWHDTP81UU", "reviewer_name": "Chanly Duong", "headline": "my review of the razor viper v3 pro", "review_text": "now for my background, i play r6 and csgo, and occasionally roblox shooters. i went from originally a 60g razer orochi v2 using a fingertip grip, and i went to this mouse with a traditional claw. i’ve had this mouse for a few months and i can say that this is a very good and universal shape for all sorts of grips. i have a medium size hand and i can comfortably fingertip and claw this mouse. the coating is lovely and the best i’ve personally felt on a mouse, and i tried the grips but they eventually wear out over time so i don’t recommend using those (the actual mouse texture is better than the grips anyway). now i know this sounds a little ridiculous but moving from a 60g small mouse not even including the batteries, i played a LOT better with this bigger one after adjusting and i’m honestly happy with my purchase (even though it cost quite a bit). it feels light in the hand for the size and the weight is flawlessly distributed. the skates are solid for being stock but you can always upgrade, the scroll wheel is pretty normal and has distinctive bumps per scroll but personally i like more smoother ones (i am probably just being nitpicky). the main clicks are lovely to hear and the little dongle included doesn’t take up too much space, i’d say only the actual cable itself does but this isn’t actually an issue. the dongle can also support up to 8k hz which isn’t necessary but it’s a “nice to have” feature and i use 2k hz myself to save battery life; speaking of battery life it’s pretty good and i suggest not using 8k since it drains it pretty fast but it lasts up to a week or two for me with regular use not charging (just remember to plug it in after use) the side buttons are a DEFINITE improvement from my old mouse and that was a perfect feature on the mouse. now, razer’s synapse software can be a little finicky sometimes but i suggest just configuring your settings and uninstalling it since it can take up some of your ram and overall performance. in conclusion, this is a really good option for gaming mice and it can fit a LOT of playstyles. this has all of the latest mouse tech (might be a little outdated for me to be saying that in the big 25 now) and each part of the mouse is very pleasant to use. i suggest this mouse if you have the money (it is pretty ehh value for money but as long as you have the funds it’s a s tier mouse)", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on March 10, 2025"}, {"review_id": "R2XYMU0FSZ470Z", "reviewer_name": "CyndiCat", "headline": "Highly recommend for competitive gamers.", "review_text": "(Review from my 15 year old son) Honestly this mouse felt SO much lighter than I thought it would. I just upgraded from the Glorious Model O- Wireless Gaming Mouse, and let me say... the upgrade was WORTH it for sure. I pretty much only play Fortnite on Keyboard and Mouse, and I was having issues with my side buttons on my old mouse. I decided it was time to upgrade since I can't have those issues happening mid-game. The Razer Viper V3 Pro, is definitely a solid upgrade. The side buttons are so much more solid than the side buttons on my old mouse. Not to mention, the response time of the clicks was faster, and the accuracy of my aim with the better sensor was so much better. The scroll wheel is also very responsive and fast which is important for Fortnite. (I was able to easily quad edit in Fortnite when using this new mouse) The wireless connectivity isn't even noticeable at all. The response time is insane for a wireless mouse, and it surprised me a lot. I don't have a lot to say about the battery life yet, as this is my first day using it. I will say though, I charged the mouse to 68%, used it for an hour in Fortnite, and the battery was only 67% afterwards. Here are the few cons I can think of: When switching from whatever mouse you currently use, it will take a few hours or even a day to adjust to the lightness of the mouse. (mainly if you played on heavier mice before) It's not anything with the mouse itself, but just a matter of adjusting to the feel of the new mouse. The mouse comes with some grip tape you can put on the mouse, which honestly looks really cool in my opinion, and it really helps with making sure your aim is as good as it can be, since your hand won't slip off the mouse. (See image) (Note: mouse is charging) Razer also has a good software which allows you to adjust the mouse to match the feel of your old one which is really helpful to make sure you don't have to COMPLETELY start over with learning a sensitivity. Overall a really good mouse, no complaints to be honest.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on April 24, 2025"}, {"review_id": "R3OBYY0K19MLH9", "reviewer_name": "yandre", "headline": "Expensive, but great mouse.", "review_text": "The Razer Viper V3 has been an excellent mouse for both gaming and everyday use. It feels very lightweight and comfortable in hand, making long sessions easy with no fatigue. The shape is simple but very ergonomic, and it works well for both claw and fingertip grip styles. Performance wise, the sensor is extremely accurate and responsive. Tracking is smooth, clicks feel crisp, and there is no noticeable delay. The wireless connection is stable and reliable, with no lag or dropouts. Battery life has also been great, lasting several days of heavy use without needing frequent charging. Build quality feels solid, and the mouse buttons and scroll wheel all feel well made. Overall, the Viper V3 delivers excellent performance, comfort, and reliability. It is a great choice for anyone looking for a high quality lightweight gaming mouse.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on February 1, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R2AEK6WIEKIFZE", "reviewer_name": "Danny", "headline": "Good claw grip mouse", "review_text": "I had a Logitech superlight and moved to the Viper v3 pro. It was the best decision that I have ever made. The mouse sensor in my opinion is more accurate the Logitech mice. The feel and texture and material of the mouse feels very nice especially the white coating option is phenomenal and has really good grip for a very low amount of weight gain. The size definitely favors mid-big hands and excels in the Claw grip. It isn't the lightest mouse on the market but it still in my opinion is more than light enough for most. The scroll wheel actually feels quite nice and i prefer it over the Logitech one. Though this mouse supports 8k polling I rarely find myself using it as it drains battery too fast, I would just use 4000/2000 if you want a high enough speed with a very long battery life. If you are looking for a high quality claw grip mouse then this is the mouse for you, if you don't have a claw grip I would recommend looking at other mice that might be for you.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on May 1, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R30EJCO7NFKGJJ", "reviewer_name": "The Lovely Lyss", "headline": "Most satisfying mouse I have ever used; full stop.", "review_text": "As someone who loves the Superlight and has been jamming out with version 2 of it along with a Logitech Pro X TKL paired with it, it's been nice to swap back to my Black Widow V4 along with the Viper Pro 3. Right out of the box, and I am someone with medium to large hands, this mouse is just a pure delight to hold; it's not often I can say that my hands feel like they disappear when using a peripheral, but this mouse and the Superlight from Logi are the two mice that achieve that for me. Razer knew what they were doing here and it shows in the product; this will be my go-to mouse and I will alternate my Razer setup back to the Logitech set up as the mood strikes me to change things up week by week. When it comes time for the Wooting 80HE to arrive, I will most likely be pairing the Viper Pro 3 with that board due to just how consistently good it feels; I am 3 hours deep into a play session and the battery is down to 98% and I'm using the 4K polling rate; not going to bother with 8K just yet. It's hard to put into words here just how good the slight ergo shape of this mouse feels; I really have tried a number of different mice and this could be \"the one\"; I don't say this in a hyperbolic fashion either. It's rare that you use a gaming device where you just forget what you're using because it seamlessly blends into the play session. For anyone looking to try this out, the asking price is steep. For a low frills mouse in the aesthetic department it really isn't going to be winning wards for it's design change to be not as sharp as it's predecessor. I for one really dig the smoother design and the light hump towards the back of the mouse, the finger ridges, or whatever you want to call them, on the L + R mouse clicks, all come together to suit whatever combination of grip you want to employ here. I am using a light palm grip and find that going claw and then relaxing my fingers feel natural. The side buttons deserve a special award here; they are separated ever so slightly and their clicks are immediate / responsive. Truly the only gripe I have with my Superlight are the side buttons; Logitech really needs to take the oatmeal mush out of those and it will be a near perfect mouse for me. Really curious to see what kind of competition this will spur with other manufacturers; that said, and for now, this is the best of the best for something that is here, on Amazon, that you can order and have by tomorrow while it's in stock. To whoever nabs one, enjoy; curious to see other reviews pop up on here.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on April 25, 2024"}, {"review_id": "R3GO5MQWET3ULK", "reviewer_name": "ludy", "headline": "Best Gaming Mouse for Claw and Fingertip grip", "review_text": "TLDR: Good mouse, great quality for price, beautiful designs, 10/10 The Razer Viper V3 Pro is probably the best gaming mouse hands down. It’s ultra lightweight, feels amazing to move around, and extremely responsive. The clicks are a little on the louder side, the material is smooth and not particularly grippy, so if you prefer grippier mice, there are those grip stickers that you can put on. I have an average adult male sized hand. In terms of what type of grip you use (claw, palm, etc..) this mouse is definitely a claw or fingertip type of mouse. Palm grip doesn’t feel amazing on this mouse since it’s a little small in my opinion. There’s also no “ergonomic” shape like the razer deathadder, so if you’re a claw or fingertip type grip person, this is probably the best mouse on the market you can get. (Please do check measurements to compare with your own hand size) I got the faker edition due to his iconic style, and it’s a beautiful red with a stunning demon art design. Overall it’s a high end mouse with high end performance, the mouse is definitely equal value to the price. For league players out there: I ranked up from Platinum to Emerald after I got this mouse (not saying it does wonders lol)", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on January 23, 2026"}, {"review_id": "RE15LEL6ZZ9UM", "reviewer_name": "Steven", "headline": "Light with great battery life", "review_text": "I have had this mouse for about a year now and use it as my daily driver, and I love it. It is really light and glides across the mouse pad. The mouse wheel is not noisy at all and neither is the clicking of the mouse buttons imo. The battery life is good lasting more than a few all day play sessions, and a couple of weeks of light use. It comes with some little adhesive pads that you can place on the mouse which I would recommend using as the mouse is very smooth. My complaints are that the mouse gets clammy feeling after a while. Not a huge deal, but I have thought of buying another adhesive pad to go over the emblem because it gets to feel gross. I do clean it, but this is the only mouse I have ever had this issue with. Also the dongle is kind of a pain if you have OCD, it is hard to get it to lay flat down. Overall I love the mouse and think it is worth the money. I would just recommend buying an adhesive patch (I'm not sure what they are really called) to go over the razer emblem as that part can start to feel gross.", "rating": "4.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 16, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R1UVWDSNDA0MC6", "reviewer_name": "R", "headline": "Surprisingly lightweight, good polling rate and no wifi-interference!", "review_text": "So far so good. I was impressed on how light this mouse felt when I used it for the first time. You can definitely feel the extra accuracy when you aim, by that I mean every small movement you make on your mousepad translates exactly as you would expect on the screen. My router and modem are right under my desk and I don't get any interference. I don't open the program that comes with it (synapse) because I used a wired headset with it (razer blackshark v2 X) and I don't want synapse messing the audio settings of my headset since the default option is pretty good. The battery works for a long time; I used it for like 3 consecutive days and when I open synapse to check battery is about 70% (I use 2k polling rate). Clicking sounds satisfying as you would expect from an expensive mouse. Your forearm gets considerably less tired. The side buttons and click buttons have not collected any dust or grime from my hands, unlike my old mouse did.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on February 1, 2026"}]

reviews: [{"review_id": "R2WEZYWH2PRQS0", "reviewer_name": "Richard", "headline": "Best Overall Mouse Out There", "review_text": "Fourth review: I did end up getting a new computer setup, and combining it with my work from home setup I had to get a wired mouse that is now my primary mouse, so I have been using my UHURU mouse much less. My other mice had issues where the thumb buttons would eventually cave in after years of abuse, but this time I think the mouse is just slowly dying. It is now kind of flickering between being on and off. I have already placed an order for another one, and will continue using this mouse until something better comes along, but it’s hard to imagine that’ll happen anytime soon. Like clockwork, these mice seem to last just over two years for me, with heavy every day use (12+ hours per day). This time, my third UHURU gaming mouse had one of the side buttons cave in, similar to my first one. I again could not be happier with my experience. For $20, you're getting an incredibly durable wireless mouse that has a very smooth feel, fits perfectly in the hand for someone with average or above average hand sizes, and looks amazing with that LED lighting and matte black casing. I can't give enough praise to UHURU for this mouse. Unless something drastically changes, I don't see myself ever using a different mouse at any point in the future. I don't think I've ever had this consistently positive of an experience with any other product on Amazon, this mouse is seriously incredible. I will be sure to come back in another two years with an update after I use my fourth UHURU gaming mouse to death. Second review: I reviewed this mouse two years ago, and had purchased it again to replace the original one I had because after two years of extensive use it finally had enough. Couldn’t have been happier with it. The replacement one I received also lasted two years for me, with extensive every day heavy gaming use. I literally use it actively for 12 hours a day or so, every day. Everything I do in life is from my computer, and this mouse has weathered that storm for two years on two separate occasions now. Last time one of the thumb buttons finally had caved in, this time it’s just slowly dying, randomly turning off while plugged in. Again, couldn’t be happier with how long it has lasted and how much it has endured. I cannot recommend this mouse enough for anyone out there, regardless of your situation. I have now ordered another one, and will update again in another two years! First review: This mouse is amazing, regardless of the price, but the price just makes it that much better. I purchased this mouse in January of 2018 and today, in April of 2020, it finally had its first problem. One of the side/thumb buttons caved in, basically, which is the result of heavy use over a long period of time. I have already placed an order for a new one, and my girlfriend is excited to use my old one since she doesn't use the side buttons and it still functions perfectly otherwise. It's hard for me to find wireless and comfortable gaming mice that have acceptable performance, but this one had it all. I can't tell the difference in delay between this wireless mouse and other wired mice. On top of it, it's very comfortable. I have a slightly above average hand size and with most mice it's hard for me to find a comfortable way to grip it and use it, but this mouse is the perfect size and I'm not having to stretch my fingers to reach any of the buttons, they're all in the perfect place. It's very responsive to movement, and unlike other wireless mice when it goes into power-save mode and you have to click to wake it up, it doesn't send a \"click\" command to the computer, so if it went into power-save mode while the cursor was over a button, it wouldn't click the button when I wake up the mouse, which brings me to its incredible battery life and charging speed. I thought for sure with the LED lights and low price the battery wouldn't last very long, but it lasts me multiple days on one charge before I need to recharge it. Then, when I need to charge it, I just plug it into my computer and it becomes a wired mouse for about 20 minutes and then it'll last me a couple more days with heavy use. The bottom line is that if you're looking for a great wireless gaming mouse at an affordable price, stop looking, you've found it. There's no reason not to get this mouse if you're a gamer. reviews: [{"review_id": "R385EMC0SNNAK3", "reviewer_name": "Amazon Customer", "headline": "Yes! Beats the G502 Hero (which I liked) and the G502 X (by a lot)", "review_text": "Good god, what a mouse. I mean, it's not perfect; nothing is. But it's so good. I came from years of the G502 Hero; the grips on it were wearing out. I first decided to try a G502 X, as it was supposed to be an improved version of the Hero, essentially. For $25 more than the Basilisk, it pretty much sucked in my opinion. The only thing I could imagine picking it over the Basilisk for is weight. But if you care that much about weight, there are much lighter mice on the market. --- I'll review it as compared to the Hero (and a bit to the X), as that's what I know. They're pretty common, so maybe this will help people out if they're thinking about converting: Initially I wasn't so sure about the grip and the main mouse buttons. The mouse buttons have a rough texture, and I found with my Hero that when my fingers were slightly tacky/damp, they would stick slightly to the surface of the buttons in the same way a clean basketball shoe does to a court (i.e., not \"sticky\", but grippy). I liked that. But after using it for a while, I think it's totally fine and maybe even better. The feet seem the same to me as the G502 X, which is good. They're white PTFE. Very smooth. The scroll wheel is *fantastic*. Like, it's perfect. It seems to control the mode with an electromagnet, so it makes a cool click sound when the computer is restarted and such. And it even has a setting in the software where you can have it tactile by default, but with a quick flick, it switches to free-spin temporarily. Awesome. And when I move the mouse quickly side to side, there is absolutely no play in the wheel. Nothing. That was one of my annoyances with the Hero. The scroll wheel would wobble audibly and tactilely when in free spin mode with even moderately fast mouse movements. The click noise isn't as nice as I expected, but it's totally fine and better than the X (which was super loud and piercing). I'd put it somewhere between the X and the Hero. It's kind of like if someone built the X and then was like, oh, that sucks, and then made adjustments like a sane human. I believe the Basilisk switches are optical (the Hero is mechanical and the X is hybrid mech/optical), and so maybe that's approximately what happened. In short, I think the Hero is a pretty quiet click, and I think the Basilisk is a very standard click. Sounds like what I'd use as a mouse click if I were a foley artist. The Basilisk's weight is listed at 101g, and it feels quite nice. Not hard to control. I'm sure I'll get even better as we go, though. The palm section is actually quite high! Like, even more than the Hero. It feels pretty good so far. The Basilisk's cable is an absolute work of art. I mean, it's perfect. It's got a soft woven sleeve and is not stiff at all. I had the same kind of reaction to it as I did when I got my current massage shower head and found that no, the tube connecting the head to the spigot doesn't actually have to be stiff at all to do its job. The software is slightly annoying because there's a separate program for the lighting and the mouse (though they're styled identically and could ostensibly be packaged in one app). But its functionality is nice. There are 9 RGB zones around the bottom edge of the mouse, plus one on the scroll wheel and the logo under the palm. They seem rather infinitely adjustable. reviews: [{"review_id": "R2YUBWHDTP81UU", "reviewer_name": "Chanly Duong", "headline": "my review of the razor viper v3 pro", "review_text": "now for my background, i play r6 and csgo, and occasionally roblox shooters. i went from originally a 60g razer orochi v2 using a fingertip grip, and i went to this mouse with a traditional claw. i’ve had this mouse for a few months and i can say that this is a very good and universal shape for all sorts of grips. i have a medium size hand and i can comfortably fingertip and claw this mouse. the coating is lovely and the best i’ve personally felt on a mouse, and i tried the grips but they eventually wear out over time so i don’t recommend using those (the actual mouse texture is better than the grips anyway). now i know this sounds a little ridiculous but moving from a 60g small mouse not even including the batteries, i played a LOT better with this bigger one after adjusting and i’m honestly happy with my purchase (even though it cost quite a bit). it feels light in the hand for the size and the weight is flawlessly distributed. the skates are solid for being stock but you can always upgrade, the scroll wheel is pretty normal and has distinctive bumps per scroll but personally i like more smoother ones (i am probably just being nitpicky). the main clicks are lovely to hear and the little dongle included doesn’t take up too much space, i’d say only the actual cable itself does but this isn’t actually an issue. the dongle can also support up to 8k hz which isn’t necessary but it’s a “nice to have” feature and i use 2k hz myself to save battery life; speaking of battery life it’s pretty good and i suggest not using 8k since it drains it pretty fast but it lasts up to a week or two for me with regular use not charging (just remember to plug it in after use) the side buttons are a DEFINITE improvement from my old mouse and that was a perfect feature on the mouse. now, razer’s synapse software can be a little finicky sometimes but i suggest just configuring your settings and uninstalling it since it can take up some of your ram and overall performance. in conclusion, this is a really good option for gaming mice and it can fit a LOT of playstyles. this has all of the latest mouse tech (might be a little outdated for me to be saying that in the big 25 now) and each part of the mouse is very pleasant to use. i suggest this mouse if you have the money (it is pretty ehh value for money but as long as you have the funds it’s a s tier mouse)", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on March 10, 2025"}, {"review_id": "R2XYMU0FSZ470Z", "reviewer_name": "CyndiCat", "headline": "Highly recommend for competitive gamers.", "review_text": "(Review from my 15 year old son) Honestly this mouse felt SO much lighter than I thought it would. I just upgraded from the Glorious Model O- Wireless Gaming Mouse, and let me say... the upgrade was WORTH it for sure. I pretty much only play Fortnite on Keyboard and Mouse, and I was having issues with my side buttons on my old mouse. I decided it was time to upgrade since I can't have those issues happening mid-game. The Razer Viper V3 Pro, is definitely a solid upgrade. The side buttons are so much more solid than the side buttons on my old mouse. Not to mention, the response time of the clicks was faster, and the accuracy of my aim with the better sensor was so much better. The scroll wheel is also very responsive and fast which is important for Fortnite. (I was able to easily quad edit in Fortnite when using this new mouse) The wireless connectivity isn't even noticeable at all. The response time is insane for a wireless mouse, and it surprised me a lot. I don't have a lot to say about the battery life yet, as this is my first day using it. I will say though, I charged the mouse to 68%, used it for an hour in Fortnite, and the battery was only 67% afterwards. Here are the few cons I can think of: When switching from whatever mouse you currently use, it will take a few hours or even a day to adjust to the lightness of the mouse. (mainly if you played on heavier mice before) It's not anything with the mouse itself, but just a matter of adjusting to the feel of the new mouse. The mouse comes with some grip tape you can put on the mouse, which honestly looks really cool in my opinion, and it really helps with making sure your aim is as good as it can be, since your hand won't slip off the mouse. (See image) (Note: mouse is charging) Razer also has a good software which allows you to adjust the mouse to match the feel of your old one which is really helpful to make sure you don't have to COMPLETELY start over with learning a sensitivity. Overall a really good mouse, no complaints to be honest.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on April 24, 2025"}, {"review_id": "R3OBYY0K19MLH9", "reviewer_name": "yandre", "headline": "Expensive, but great mouse.", "review_text": "The Razer Viper V3 has been an excellent mouse for both gaming and everyday use. It feels very lightweight and comfortable in hand, making long sessions easy with no fatigue. The shape is simple but very ergonomic, and it works well for both claw and fingertip grip styles. It is a great choice for anyone looking for a high quality lightweight gaming mouse.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on February 1, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R2AEK6WIEKIFZE", "reviewer_name": "Danny", "headline": "Good claw grip mouse", "review_text": "I had a Logitech superlight and moved to the Viper v3 pro. It was the best decision that I have ever made. The mouse sensor in my opinion is more accurate the Logitech mice. The feel and texture and material of the mouse feels very nice especially the white coating option is phenomenal and has really good grip for a very low amount of weight gain. The size definitely favors mid-big hands and excels in the Claw grip. It isn't the lightest mouse on the market but it still in my opinion is more than light enough for most. The scroll wheel actually feels quite nice and i prefer it over the Logitech one. Though this mouse supports 8k polling I rarely find myself using it as it drains battery too fast, I would just use 4000/2000 if you want a high enough speed with a very long battery life. If you are looking for a high quality claw grip mouse then this is the mouse for you, if you don't have a claw grip I would recommend looking at other mice that might be for you.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on May 1, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R30EJCO7NFKGJJ", "reviewer_name": "The Lovely Lyss", "headline": "Most satisfying mouse I have ever used; full stop.", "review_text": "As someone who loves the Superlight and has been jamming out with version 2 of it along with a Logitech Pro X TKL paired with it, it's been nice to swap back to my Black Widow V4 along with the Viper Pro 3. Right out of the box, and I am someone with medium to large hands, this mouse is just a pure delight to hold; it's not often I can say that my hands feel like they disappear when using a peripheral, but this mouse and the Superlight from Logi are the two mice that achieve that for me. Razer knew what they were doing here and it shows in the product; this will be my go-to mouse and I will alternate my Razer setup back to the Logitech set up as the mood strikes me to change things up week by week. When it comes time for the Wooting 80HE to arrive, I will most likely be pairing the Viper Pro 3 with that board due to just how consistently good it feels; I am 3 hours deep into a play session and the battery is down to 98% and I'm using the 4K polling rate; not going to bother with 8K just yet. It's hard to put into words here just how good the slight ergo shape of this mouse feels; I really have tried a number of different mice and this could be \"the one\"; I don't say this in a hyperbolic fashion either. It's rare that you use a gaming device where you just forget what you're using because it seamlessly blends into the play session. For anyone looking to try this out, the asking price is steep. For a low frills mouse in the aesthetic department it really isn't going to be winning wards for it's design change to be not as sharp as it's predecessor. I for one really dig the smoother design and the light hump towards the back of the mouse, the finger ridges, or whatever you want to call them, on the L + R mouse clicks, all come together to suit whatever combination of grip you want to employ here. I am using a light palm grip and find that going claw and then relaxing my fingers feel natural. The side buttons deserve a special award here; they are separated ever so slightly and their clicks are immediate / responsive. Truly the only gripe I have with my Superlight are the side buttons; Logitech really needs to take the oatmeal mush out of those and it will be a near perfect mouse for me. Really curious to see what kind of competition this will spur with other manufacturers; that said, and for now, this is the best of the best for something that is here, on Amazon, that you can order and have by tomorrow while it's in stock. To whoever nabs one, enjoy; curious to see other reviews pop up on here.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on April 25, 2024"}, {"review_id": "R3GO5MQWET3ULK", "reviewer_name": "ludy", "headline": "Best Gaming Mouse for Claw and Fingertip grip", "review_text": "TLDR: Good mouse, great quality for price, beautiful designs, 10/10 The Razer Viper V3 Pro is probably the best gaming mouse hands down. It’s ultra lightweight, feels amazing to move around, and extremely responsive. The clicks are a little on the louder side, the material is smooth and not particularly grippy, so if you prefer grippier mice, there are those grip stickers that you can put on. I have an average adult male sized hand. In terms of what type of grip you use (claw, palm, etc..) this mouse is definitely a claw or fingertip type of mouse. Palm grip doesn’t feel amazing on this mouse since it’s a little small in my opinion. There’s also no “ergonomic” shape like the razer deathadder, so if you’re a claw or fingertip type grip person, this is probably the best mouse on the market you can get. (Please do check measurements to compare with your own hand size) I got the faker edition due to his iconic style, and it’s a beautiful red with a stunning demon art design. Overall it’s a high end mouse with high end performance, the mouse is definitely equal value to the price. For league players out there: I ranked up from Platinum to Emerald after I got this mouse (not saying it does wonders lol)", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on January 23, 2026"}, {"review_id": "RE15LEL6ZZ9UM", "reviewer_name": "Steven", "headline": "Light with great battery life", "review_text": "I have had this mouse for about a year now and use it as my daily driver, and I love it. It is really light and glides across the mouse pad. The mouse wheel is not noisy at all and neither is the clicking of the mouse buttons imo. The battery life is good lasting more than a few all day play sessions, and a couple of weeks of light use. It comes with some little adhesive pads that you can place on the mouse which I would recommend using as the mouse is very smooth. My complaints are that the mouse gets clammy feeling after a while. Not a huge deal, but I have thought of buying another adhesive pad to go over the emblem because it gets to feel gross. I do clean it, but this is the only mouse I have ever had this issue with. Also the dongle is kind of a pain if you have OCD, it is hard to get it to lay flat down. Overall I love the mouse and think it is worth the money. I would just recommend buying an adhesive patch (I'm not sure what they are really called) to go over the razer emblem as that part can start to feel gross.", "rating": "4.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 16, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R1UVWDSNDA0MC6", "reviewer_name": "R", "headline": "Surprisingly lightweight, good polling rate and no wifi-interference!", "review_text": "So far so good. I was impressed on how light this mouse felt when I used it for the first time. You can definitely feel the extra accuracy when you aim, by that I mean every small movement you make on your mousepad translates exactly as you would expect on the screen. My router and modem are right under my desk and I don't get any interference. I don't open the program that comes with it (synapse) because I used a wired headset with it (razer blackshark v2 X) and I don't want synapse messing the audio settings of my headset since the default option is pretty good. It allows you to flick quickly, and track targets consistently, which is where my claim of \"natural aim bot\" came from. It's not too light where you might find yourself tensing up too much to keep it in place, but if you came from a heavier mouse, then you might overflick your target a few times. The features the mouse offered through Razer's Synapse software such as the DPI and mappings are very useful. You can set different profiles for different games, so there are different DPI's for each game. In addition, you can change the mouse's buttons to be mapped to keys on your keyboard. I have been using the mouse for 12 days at 1000hz (sometimes 8000, but only for a couple of Apex matches) and it has only gone down to 60%. On top of all of that, Razer has finally made a web software. On paper, the V4 Pro has many improvements, but the only real upgrade that a player will notice is the battery life and the web software. The first negative is the price is steep, especially when you could get the V3 Pro Se for like have the price. Two, the M1/M2 switches are on the loud side, but you won't notice them with headphones. I have a LITE-ON USB 2.0 External CD/DVD Writer Model eUAU108, manufactured in 2013, with an attached cable that is slightly less than 4 inches long. This model was an improvement over prior models, in that it requires only a single USB 2.0 connection, whereas previous models employed a Y-cable to enable connecting to 2 USB ports simultaneously for additional power. I have always felt that this drive was marginally capable of running on the 500 mA specification for USB 2.0 ports. I think this is the main reason for the ultra short cable - to minimize the voltage drop. The short cable worked OK when I was using the drive with a laptop, but attempting to use it with a computer attached to the back of my flat screen monitor is a major problem. The USB ports are about a foot above the desktop, making it necessary to support the drive in some manner. This has always been problematic. I tried using the only USB extension cable that I had, a cheap dollar store cable, and it did not work at all. My next thought was that I should purchase a higher quality, and obviously more expensive, USB cable, but I still had reservations. Would a longer cable, even of a higher quality, work? Why did LITE-ON force a short cable onto the consumer? They could have provided a USB port instead of an attached cable. I then thought of using a powered hub, which could solve the voltage/power issue, but I still wondered if there might be other signal quality issues that a longer cable might cause. I believe I was starting to overthink the matter at this point! I started looking at the market of powered hubs and discovered that there was quite a variety, from no-name cheapies to surprisingly expensive higher end units. It was easy to eliminate the no-name cheapies because there were brand names I was familiar with that were very affordable. Then I discovered that some of the hubs were rated at 10 Gbps! Gotta have that feature, right? Even though I don't have a single device faster than 5 Gbps, I justified this feature on the basis of future-proofing. I figured it would only be a matter of time before I had devices of that speed. Later on I discovered that all the USB ports on the computer attached to the back of my monitor are 10 Gbps capable – five are USB 3.2 Gen2 (10 Gbps) and one is USB4 (40 Gbps!) - additional justification for going with a 10 Gbps hub. As I looked at the 10 Gbps offerings I quickly discovered that many, if not most of them, were from RSHTECH/Rosonway. They have quite a variety of well designed, useful devices. So many options that I found it helpful to generate a table of features to more easily compare them. I finally decided to go with the RSH-H7C4 for the following reasons: • 10 Gbps on every port • both USB-A and USB-C ports • push button switch (vs. rocker type), with an indicator light, for each port • all ports support USB Battery Charging 1.2 protocol (BC1.2), delivering a maximum of 1.5A at 5V (7.5W) per port [standard USB ports limit current to 0.5A (USB 2.0) or 0.9A (USB 3.2)] • 36W (12V/3A) DC power adapter • detachable 3.3 foot USB-C host cable (when I need to connect to a USB-A host I use a cheap adapter I purchased at a dollar store; some of the Rosonway units include a dual-headed cable with both A and C plugs!) • two year warranty It's a beautifully designed unit with a solid, weighty feel to it. Rounded edges and a thin accent band of non-anodized aluminum around each end give this hub a modern, classy appearance. With the case being narrow and slightly rounded on the bottom, one might have concern about its stability against the pushing and pulling of the connected USB cables. While it might technically be more stable with a completely flat bottom, it is surprisingly stable as is due to its weight and mass. Not at all like some of the lighter weight plastic cased devices that I have. It would take a deliberate effort to tip it over; I don't think that will be an issue. I actually do tip it over to accommodate one of my situations: the cable on my DVD drive is so short that the drive cannot lay flat when the cable is inserted into the port on the hub from above. I have to lay the hub on its side (see video). The included USB cable is heavy gauge, very thick. With my limited experience in the world of USB cables I have made two observations: 1)there is a tremendous range of cost, quality, and capabilities among the many cables on the market; 2)an extra USB cable frequently comes in handy. It would make sense to me that RSHTECH would provide a suitably high-grade cable with their hub in order to support the 10 Gbps data rate and the BC1.2 current draw capability. The fact that the USB cable is detachable is a bonus! It can be used elsewhere. I could even change it into an extension cable by the use of a gender-changing adapter. The indicator lights are a beautiful blue, quite small, but tastefull in my opinion; apparently too small for some reviewers, but I have no complaint. I would rather have them understated than overstated. The first testing I did was to connect the aforementioned LITE-ON CD/DVD writer to the computer hanging on the back of my monitor using the RSH-H7C4 hub and its included USB cable. (When the LITE-ON drive is directly attached to this computer I never have problems because the power requirement of the LITE-ON drive is easily satisfied.) I briefly tried the hub in “bus-powered” mode (without the power supply attached). I was able to read files on the DVD writer with no problem. (This was just a brief, not comprehensive, test because my main concern was testing the more power intensive task of burning a disk.) The next testing was in “self-powered” mode (with the power supply attached). I successfully burned and verified an ISO image. I then disconnected the power supply and tried to burn the image again in bus-powered mode. The burning went without any error messages, but the verification process failed. Another attempt in bus-powered mode failed during the burning process. Returning to self-powered mode (with the power supply attached), I was again able to successfully burn and verify the ISO image. It appears that when the DVD writer is attached through the hub and cable, burning a disk requires additional power beyond what the computer port is supplying (in order to power the circuitry in the hub and to compensate for loss over the length of the three foot cable). USB Battery Charging 1.2 protocol (BC1.2) seems to do the job here. I am pleased with that! I have solved the short cable issue; I can now lay my DVD drive flat on the desk and have dependable operation. Additional testing with a much older computer, a Dell Inspiron Mini 1012 (vintage 2010), revealed an unexpected limitation: the DVD writer was unable to be recognized as a boot device by the Inspiron Mini when connected to it through the hub. As far as I can tell, this is a limitation of the older BIOS in the Inspiron. There is no way to make this system recognize an optical drive connected via a USB hub at boot up. After the system is booted the drive is able to be used with no problem. It is my understanding that the more modern BIOSes of today handle this situation in a more sophisticated manner and can detect hub-connected optical drives at bootup. I verified this by bootup tests on the computer attached to my monitor and on a modern netbook. Both of those systems were able to recognize the DVD writer at bootup with no problem when it was connected via the hub. The Dell Inspiron Mini 1012 has USB 2.0 ports that theoretically should supply enough power for the LITE-ON CD/DVD writer, but I have always felt that it was marginal. I would like to be able to supplement the power. The RSH-H7C4 is only a partial solution here. It can be used with the Inspiron for burning disks since that is a process that occurs after bootup, but in the case where I need to boot from this DVD writer I might have to first transfer the DVD image to a bootable USB thumb drive and use that instead. While not a comprehensive evaluation of the RSH-H7C4, my tests have assured me that some of my problems have been solved. I can comfortably lay the LITE-ON CD/DVD writer on the desk instead of trying to figure out how to suspend it a foot up in the air in order to attach it to the computer hanging behind my flat screen monitor. I can also use the hub for more dependable disk burning using my Inspiron Mini 1012. I am quite impressed with the RSH-H7C4 hub and RSHTECH/Rosonway. I've always been very excited by little “boxes” and devices that solve computer interconnection (and other) problems. The companies that come up with these solutions are frequently very clever. RSHTECH will now be one of the first companies I look to for such solutions. A brief look at their lineup shows devices such as: • USB switches (to share USB ports between two computers) • powered and unpowered USB hubs, some with card readers and HDMI ports • powered USB extension cables • unpowered USB extension cables with built-in signal booster chips • USB HDD/SSD enclosures • docking and cloning stations • 10 Gbps USB connected M.2 NVME/SATA SSD enclosures • 10 Gbps USB connected Magnetic M.2 NVME SSD enclosure with 100W PD RSHTECH puts an effort into including enough hard facts and specifications in their product descriptions to enable consumers to easily understand a device’s capabilities and limitations. I have also been burned enough times by bad ones to approach any new hub with a healthy dose of skepticism. So when I say that the Rosonway powered USB hub has genuinely impressed me, I want you to understand that it is coming from someone who does not hand out compliments to peripheral hardware easily. I have had this hub for 13 days now. That might not sound like a long time, but in the context of my daily IT work, I have put it through what I would consider a serious run of testing. This is not a hub that has been sitting on a desk powering a wireless mouse dongle and a phone charger. It has been put through a ringer of a minimum of 12-14 hours 5-6 days a week. And it was used every day. With a rotating cast of demanding devices that would expose any weakness in a lesser product. Why I Came Back to Rosonway This is actually my second Rosonway hub. My first one is still running, still reliable, and was purchased specifically because I had grown so frustrated with other brands that I needed something I could actually count on. Before finding Rosonway the first time, I dealt with pretty much every problem a USB hub can throw at you — and often all at once. Devices dropping connection randomly. Transfer speeds that had no business being as slow as they were, even on a nominally high-speed hub. Units that died within weeks of purchase. Build quality that felt like it might give out at any moment. When you work in IT, unreliable hardware is not just an annoyance — it is a productivity problem and, at times, a professional one. The last thing I need in the middle of a task is a hub that decides to drop a device or throttle my speeds without warning. After going through several different brands and experiencing those issues repeatedly, I finally landed on Rosonway. My first unit solved all of those problems and has kept solving them ever since. So when I needed more ports, the decision to go back to Rosonway was not really a decision at all. It was the obvious move based on earned trust. Sure you could go with more notorious brands, but the bang for my buck on this brand has been optimal. Daily Use in an IT Context My use case is not casual. I run this hub daily as part of an IT work setup that includes both a PC and a Mac, and I switch between the two regularly. Cross-platform reliability is something I specifically look for and specifically test, because a hub that works beautifully on Windows but causes headaches on macOS is only solving half my problem. This one works correctly on both. No configuration differences, no quirks on one platform that do not exist on the other. It simply works the same way on both machines, which is exactly what you want. The range of peripherals I have connected through this hub over the past 13 days is wide. I have been running a wired USB-C to 3.5mm DAC for my Corsair headset with microphone — and I want to flag this one specifically, because audio devices are often where cheaper hubs start to show their weaknesses. A DAC demands consistent, clean power delivery. Any instability shows up immediately as audio dropout, static, or microphone signal issues. This hub has delivered clean, uninterrupted audio and microphone performance every single time. Beyond that, I have put external hard drives, thumb drives, and an SSD dock through this hub. External drives and SSD docks are about the most demanding things you can connect to a USB hub from a power and bandwidth standpoint. Drives pulling sustained power while transferring data will expose any inadequacy in a hub's power management quickly. I have had no issues — transfers run at expected speeds, the SSD dock behaves as if it is connected directly to the machine, and nothing has dropped or stuttered. I have connected all of these devices in various combinations, not just one at a time. Running multiple demanding peripherals simultaneously is where a lot of hubs start to fall apart, and this one has handled every configuration I have thrown at it without complaint. No Drivers, No Nonsense One of the things I appreciated immediately was the plug-and-play experience. There were no extra drivers to hunt down and install. I will give the manufacturer points for build quality, the hub seems to built well and using quality materials. Unfortunately, that's about where the positive news ends and as far as usability goes I cannot recommend this device. I've listed below the problems I experienced within the first 24 hours of usage: 1) The switches outright just do not work for many devices. I tried several devices which seem to somehow just \"ignore\" the switch being turned off. I put ignore in quotes, because the device should not be built in a way that would allow any attached device to communicate with the host while it's off. For some devices, the switch does work correctly. However, for other devices, I can plug a USB cable into the hub and have it persistently connected to the host no matter how many times I toggle the switch on and off. This is a key indicator that the device was not designed in a secure way. When the toggle switch is off, power and connectivity should be completely disconnected to the port. The fact that I am able to bypass the toggle switch is an indicator that some sort of firmware workaround is being used. Bad news here. 2) Power delivery does not seem to work correctly on the hub. I'm using the power adapter that was delivered with the device which is plugged into a stable power source. Some devices which require power delivery (USB-PD) get stuck in an initializing state when drawing power from the hub. They get enough power to appear powered on, but the device never initializes and the host system can detect something was plugged in but cannot interface with the device. When I switch these devices to a different hub (or directly to the host), the issue is not present and the device works as expected. 3) Even devices that do connect, seem to have issues with performance and/or connectivity. When some devices are attached to the hub, the host operating system seems to hang while the device is connecting. I experience this on about 1/3 of my attempts with any mass storage device, and some devices fairly consistently. When I do get a device to connect to the host, my transfer speeds are considerably lower than if I had used a different hub or connected directly to the host. All in all, I absolutely do not recommend this device. There are several clear indicators of poor and unsafe design when it comes to this hub, and I would not trust that it delivers power cleanly or that there's any consistent integrity on file transfers. Again, all of these issues were experienced within the first 24 hours of usage. I tested over a dozen different devices with this hub, of varying types and manufacturer. If I had this many issues straight away, I can guarantee it's not an isolated incident. Even if my hub was \"defective\", there's no way it would have been defective in a way that would selectively allow some devices to connect while toggled off. Primarily bought for the power PD through and USB-C connection which perform ok for travel with iPad.", "rating": "4.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 20, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R2U654XJZUW0JC", "reviewer_name": "A Fraser", "headline": "The Travel Dock in My Laptop Bag", "review_text": "What I like Plug-and-play. One USB-C cable in, several ports out. No drivers, no setup, no configuration. HDMI output for plugging into a hotel-room TV or conference projector without an adapter. SD card reader for moving photos off a camera. The microSD reader is a bonus. Two USB-A ports are enough for a mouse, a USB stick, or a card reader I already own. 85 W pass-through charging means I can keep my laptop charged through the hub when I have a USB-C charger handy. Lives in the laptop bag and is ready when I travel. It is the kind of accessory that pays for itself the first time you really need it. Compact and light. I forget it is in the bag until I need it. What annoys me Not a daily driver on my home desk. My home computers already have the ports I need, so the hub sits in the bag most of the time. Bus-powered. No battery, no separate power input. I am not trying to power a hungry external device through it, so this is fine, but it is not a “real docking station” with its own power supply. One HDMI output. If I wanted to drive two external monitors, I would need a different hub or a dock with display-multiplication support. The transcript says “second HDMI port,” and this hub gives me one, not two. No Ethernet port. Wireless works almost everywhere I travel, but a wired Ethernet jack would be a real bonus on hotel networks that block Wi-Fi or charge for it. I do not actually use it on my Mac mini. It would work, but I have not built the habit of plugging the mini through the hub. That is a me problem, not an Anker problem. Who it is for, and who should skip it If you travel with a laptop and need HDMI, an SD card reader, extra USB-A, and the option to charge the laptop through a single cable, this is the right tool. It is small enough to leave in the bag and useful enough to justify its weight. Skip it if you want a full desktop dock with its own power supply, multiple display outputs, Ethernet, and the ability to drive a multi-monitor workstation. That is a different product class, and a single USB-C hub with bus power will not do that job. Skip it if your laptop already has every port you need. The hub is solving a missing-port problem, and if you do not have one, it will just sit in your bag. Verdict The Anker USB-C 7-in-1 hub is a small, useful travel accessory that lives in my laptop bag and earns its place every time I take a trip. It is not exciting. It is not a daily driver. It is the kind of thing that disappears into your workflow and then you are grateful for it when you need it. Grade: A—if you want a single-cable travel dock for a laptop or Mac mini. A Few Minor Considerations: While I'm extremely happy with the Anker USB-C Hub, there are a couple of minor drawbacks that I've seen mentioned in other reviews: Limited Ethernet: Some users have expressed a desire for an Ethernet port on the hub. Can Get Warm: A few reviewers have mentioned that the hub can get a bit warm during use, especially when transferring large files or using the HDMI port. We have tried a number of USB Docks over the years: some were good; others not so much. So in searching currently available docks, I ran across this one that Amazon kinda of co-branded. Overall Impression I was intrigued because it had a 10 Gbps network connection. That would allow me to make full use of my fiber connection. It also had a 4K HDMI port, good for my 4K monitors. And two high-speed USB connections. This is just enough of everything we typically need/use. I run on a MacBook Pro M3 rich in memory and disk space. When I tested it, I was running Sonoma 14.7 with Sequoia 15.0 having just come available. I never use first release of major OSes, preferring to wait until the .1 release comes along. This gives others time to find the bugs and the vendor to fix them. I plugged it into my Mac. macOS asked for permission to connect the device which I gave it. macOS was happy with the device. I plugged in my monitor's HDMI cable; it connected right up. I plugged in my network cable; it too came right up. I plugged in my Logitech antenna for the detached KB/mouse; that worked. So far, so good. I plugged in a thumb drive and ... nothing. Hmm: that's odd. Plugged it into my Mac directly; worked like a champ. Plugged it back into the dock ... nothing.
