Then I noticed that my 27\" 4K LG monitor would randomly turn black, just for a second or two, then would come back on. Okay: that's weird. So I used it a bit and the monitor would turn black now and this in the middle of using it as my main/primary display. It was not like I was pushing out rapid changes such as one would do in a game. The monitor went back to being solidly on. My thumb drive showed up just like it should. My external KB/mouse worked like they always have. reviews: [{"review_id": "R13P11GN4QXLH5", "reviewer_name": "Pablo Ladino", "headline": "A huge upgrade from my BlackWidow V3", "review_text": "I honestly didn’t expect to like this keyboard this much. I upgraded from a Razer BlackWidow V3, and the difference is immediately noticeable. The magnetic switches feel incredibly smooth and responsive, and being able to adjust the actuation point and use Rapid Trigger is a game changer for competitive gaming. Movement feels much more precise, especially in Fortnite. The keyboard also feels extremely well built and premium. What I really like is that it isn’t only great for gaming. For everyday use, studying, and programming, I can switch to a normal profile and it feels just as good to type on. I was a little skeptical at first because I was already happy with my BlackWidow V3, but after using this one, I don’t think I could go back to a traditional mechanical keyboard. If you’re coming from a regular mechanical keyboard, this is a serious upgrade. Absolutely love it so far. 🔥", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 18, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R3C83LRI9YSFII", "reviewer_name": "HikerBrian", "headline": "Incredible for coding, even better for gaming,", "review_text": "This one gets reviewed from two angles. As a professional software engineer I live by the quality of my keyboard and have been opinionated about keyboards for more than 20 years, so I ran this as my daily driver for a week to test it out. It was quiet, consistent, and responsive. Despite the gaming branding, this is probably the best tenkeyless keyboard I've ever typed on. Turn the lighting off and it can be dropped onto any office desk without getting a second glance. The high quality PBT keycaps have a texture that doesn't go slick and greasy, and they shouldn't shine up the way ABS does after a few months of heavy use. The switches are factory lubed with a dense foam layer underneath, so there's no hollow plastic rattle and no metallic ping. It's also not the clicking like you get from mechanical switches. It's a low, dull sound that doesn't get annoying in a quiet room or on a call. The adjustable actuation mattered more than I expected for office use. Setting it deeper than a gamer would means you stop firing off accidental characters when your fingers graze the home row, which is something that makes most fast-actuation boards frustrating for long-form writing and code. The aluminum top gives it a solid build, so it doesn't flex or walk across the desk, and the detachable USB-C cable means a longer lifespan. After my week ended I handed it to my teenage son, the gamer, and I really don't think I'm getting it back. He found things I never would have. Rapid Trigger resets the key the instant it starts to rise instead of waiting for a fixed point, which he says completely changes counter-strafing. Snap Tap prioritizes whichever direction key you pressed most recently, so pressing A while holding D doesn't leave you standing there. Dynamic Keystroke lets a single key fire up to four different actions depending on how far down you press it, and Snap Flex assigns one action on press and a different one on release. He set up a key that peeks a corner on a light press and pulls back on release. I didn't even know keyboards did that, but he's raving about it. The 8000Hz polling means it reports to the PC eight times more often than a standard board. He swears he can feel it. I'm skeptical it's perceptible, but he's the one winning matches. All of the tuning lives in the browser based software, which allows you to adjust lighting, actuation and keybinds without installing anything. I really only had two very minor complaints about this keyboard. The switches aren't hot-swappable. Every switch fails eventually, even fancy magnetic switches rated at millions of actuations, and at this price it's disappointing that there's no path to replacing one when it does. The other is the calibration routine that needs to be run every time it's installed or keycaps are replaced, because that part of the software is just tedious and could be better designed. Those are very minor gripes against everything else here. This is a fantastic keyboard, and I'd recommend it without hesitation. Whether you're a professional keyboarder and are looking for a great tenkeyless for daily use, or a gamer looking for an edge, you really can't go wrong with this thing.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 12, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R3R6888Q0XQRNA", "reviewer_name": "NhutDuong", "headline": "Good", "review_text": "Good", "rating": "4.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 26, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R1VYXP6E9YS06X", "reviewer_name": "AmazonReviewer", "headline": "Love the design and layout, and the HE switches feels great! I also love the keycaps texture!", "review_text": "I have multiple razer keyboards from down to the 2010 black widow which is still going strong, and a few newer ones from last year and I love them, but when I saw this new huntsman V3 HE 65% keyboard I wanted to see how it was. Overall, I really like this keyboard, I love the 65% layout and the clean design it has, and the build quality is solid, and the features it has is great like the gamepad mode, sure it needs Synapse to customize the settings but I really never had issues with the software even on my other keyboards and mouses and I do like it, call me lucky I don't know, I also like that it came with a really nice 6 foot braided cord which is long enough to reach from my PC way behind my monitor with more to spare. So if you love the design and the 65% layout and hall effect switches, the value you get from this keyboard is great in my opinion, so it does get a solid 5 stars from me, I haven't had an issue yet and I had it for a couple weeks now👍", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 11, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R21G39SN8YNLHW", "reviewer_name": "MK", "headline": "Razer’s Hall Effect Switches Are a Major Improvement", "review_text": "Razer has made adjustable-actuation keyboards before, but its previous analog Huntsman models relied on optical switches. This is its first real move into the Hall effect keyboard space, and the switch change is not just a spec-sheet distinction. These new magnetic switches feel noticeably smoother and less scratchy than the optical analog switches I have used in the past, especially when pressing a key slowly or typing for longer periods. They also retain a full 4.0mm range of travel, which is less common than I expected among Hall effect gaming keyboards. I can set a very shallow actuation point for movement keys in competitive games without making the entire board feel like a hair trigger. For typing, I prefer a deeper actuation and the full key travel because it feels more natural and gives me fewer accidental inputs. That flexibility makes the Huntsman V3 HE easier to live with as an everyday keyboard rather than something designed exclusively for ranked matches. Rapid trigger works as expected, resetting each key based on movement rather than waiting for it to return to a fixed reset point. In shooters, directional inputs feel crisp and immediate, particularly when rapidly stopping, strafing, or changing direction. Snap Tap can prioritize the newest input between two movement keys, while Snap Flex adds another way to activate commands based on releasing a key. These features will matter most to serious FPS players, but the adjustable actuation is useful even outside competitive gaming. The 8000Hz polling rate gives the keyboard plenty of performance headroom. I cannot pretend the jump from an already fast gaming keyboard is transformative in every game, but inputs feel consistently immediate, and there is no sense that the keyboard is holding anything back. It is also possible to store multiple profiles, which is useful when I want aggressive gaming settings without using those same settings while typing or programming. I generally like the 65% layout because it leaves much more space for the mouse while retaining dedicated arrow keys. It is compact enough for an FPS setup without feeling as restrictive as a 60% board, although anyone who regularly uses the function row, navigation cluster, or numpad should expect a period of adjustment. The secondary functions are manageable, but they are still secondary functions. Build quality is appropriately solid for the price. The aluminum top case gives the board a sturdy feel, the doubleshot PBT keycaps have a pleasant texture, and the detachable USB-C cable makes it easier to pack or replace the cable later. The switches sound and feel much more refined than Razer’s earlier analog optical boards, though this is still a gaming keyboard rather than a heavily dampened custom mechanical board. At $120, this is competitively priced for a Hall effect keyboard from a major gaming brand, especially with 8000Hz polling, rapid trigger, adjustable actuation, onboard profiles, and a full 4.0mm travel range. The real improvement for me is not one headline feature but how much better these magnetic switches feel. They are fast enough for competitive play, smooth enough to enjoy, and versatile enough that I can type on the keyboard all day without wishing I had switched back to a conventional mechanical board.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 4, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R1OIJ117WLELF", "reviewer_name": "Amazon Customer", "headline": "Hall Effect Makes The Difference", "review_text": "Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic TKL 8KHz Wired Gaming Keyboard | Hall Effect Magnetic Switches, 8000 Hz Polling, Razer Snap Flex,Razer Snap Tap, Rapid Trigger, Adjustable Actuation So this listing is for the v3 ten key less Hunstman v3 8K HE keyboard specifically designed for gaming with hall effect switches and snap tap actions. Overall I'm very happy with my purchase", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 9, 2026"}, {"review_id": "RQL75GJKVLF7Z", "reviewer_name": "Adam Darling", "headline": "Elite Magnetic TKL Keyboard With Precision Control", "review_text": "The Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic Tenkeyless is engineered as a competitive‐grade keyboard built around Hall Effect Magnetic Switches, offering adjustable actuation from 0.1 mm to 4.0 mm and a 100‐million keystroke lifespan (). This switch architecture eliminates debounce delay entirely, enabling instantaneous actuation and reset behavior that mechanical switches simply cannot match. The magnetic sensing provides exceptionally consistent input recognition, and the keyboard’s internal calibration system compensates for magnetic interference to maintain stable performance over time. Combined with the TKL layout, which frees up desk space for low‐sensitivity mouse movement, the Huntsman V3 HE is clearly designed for players who rely on precision micro‐adjustments and rapid directional changes. One of the most defining features is Rapid Trigger, which allows keys to reset the moment they begin to rise rather than waiting for a fixed reset point. This dramatically increases responsiveness in FPS titles, enabling faster counter‐strafes, smoother movement corrections, and more reliable repeated inputs. Esports.gg’s testing highlights how Rapid Trigger transforms WASD control, making movement feel “snappy, predictable, and extremely responsive” — a sentiment that aligns with real‐world gameplay impressions. The keyboard also supports Dynamic Keystroke, allowing up to four actions on a single key at different actuation depths, and Snap Flex, which assigns one action on press and another on release. These features give competitive players granular control over movement, utility activation, and complex keybind setups, especially in games like Valorant, CS2, and Apex Legends (). The Huntsman V3 HE’s 8000 Hz HyperPolling is another major technical advantage. With true 8000 Hz performance, the keyboard sends input data to the PC eight times more frequently than standard 1000 Hz keyboards, reducing average latency to 0.60 ms — roughly 8% faster than competing high‐end boards (). In fast‐paced shooters, this reduction in input delay contributes to more immediate movement and firing responses. Esports.gg’s analysis notes that the keyboard feels “instantaneous,” with no perceptible delay between keypress and on‐screen action. For competitive players who rely on tight timing windows, this level of responsiveness provides a measurable advantage. Build quality is another strong point. The keyboard uses a 5052 aluminum alloy top case, which gives it a rigid, premium feel while keeping weight manageable for LAN events. The switches are factory‐lubricated, and a dense internal foam layer improves acoustics, reducing hollow resonance and delivering a smoother, more muted sound profile. The doubleshot PBT keycaps resist shine and wear, maintaining texture even under heavy daily use. The detachable USB‐C cable and hybrid onboard storage for up to six profiles add practical flexibility, especially for players who switch between systems or travel frequently (). Razer’s software approach is also noteworthy. The Huntsman V3 HE supports Synapse for Web, allowing users to adjust actuation, Rapid Trigger sensitivity, polling rate, lighting, and keybinds directly through a browser without installing software — ideal for tournament environments or shared PCs. The keyboard’s Chroma RGB is bright and evenly diffused, and while lighting is not the focus of this model, it integrates cleanly with competitive setups. Real‐world impressions consistently highlight the keyboard’s stability, predictable actuation behavior, and the immediate improvement in movement control during gameplay. Overall, the Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic Tenkeyless delivers exceptional responsiveness, deep customization, durable construction, and esports‐grade precision. Its combination of Hall Effect Magnetic Switches, Rapid Trigger, Dynamic Keystroke, Snap Tap, and true 8000 Hz HyperPolling makes it one of the most technically advanced competitive keyboards available. For players who prioritize movement accuracy, instant input recognition, and customizable actuation, this keyboard offers a genuine performance advantage that is immediately noticeable in high‐speed FPS environments.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 2, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R38HCBDIW4X7RK", "reviewer_name": "Terrorgod", "headline": "Maybe im ready to give Razer another chance", "review_text": "The Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic Mini keyboard is the latest addition to their Hall Effect Magnetic keyboard lineup. If you haven't been keeping up with keyboard technologies, compared to traditional keyboard switches made by companies like Cherry, they are now utilizing magnets and lasers to create a much more responsive key press reducing latency and allowing for customizable key actuation based on the users preference. I am a hobbyist with keyboard tech, where I have built a good variety of keyboards with DIY kits, customized some of my own, and tend to go out of my way to try new technologies. This is my third time trying a Hall Effect keyboard, with my first being the Steelseries Apex Pro ( with HyperMagnetic switches) and the original Razer Huntsman. I didn't hold onto either of those keyboards very long as at the time they were very expensive compared to their traditional counterparts. They also didn't wow me out of the box with their switch technology. Keypresses felt weak, as if there was no feedback to register that I had hit a key. It also took a lot of tweaking to get them to what I would consider a usable state with accurate typing. Which leaves me with the new Razer Huntsman, where I am happy to report it doesn't share any of these problems. The recent revisions have made many changes, improving the texture on the keycaps, the sound of the keypresses, the out of box actuation is exactly what I want, and the 8khz polling is probably helping with how responsive the keys feel. I generally use full size keyboards as I like to have a numpad, but the feel of this keyboard is winning me over to make it my daily driver away from my Mountain Everest Max with Cherry Blues. Lubed Holy Panda switches are the only ones I own that might feel a little bit better than these, but the overall responsiveness of these HE Magentics is something I haven't had the pleasure of experiencing before. My closing statement will be that I started my PC peripheral journey with Razer back when they released the first Blackwidow keyboard & OG Razer Naga. I have watched their products go through sharp declines, and had a time of regret after recommending them to several friends and watching their mice break down on them within a year each. I am hesitant to recommend them again due to the many issues I have had across a few years before ultimately moving away from their products entirely. This is its first real move into the Hall effect keyboard space, and the switch change is not just a spec-sheet distinction. These new magnetic switches feel noticeably smoother and less scratchy than the optical analog switches I have used in the past, especially when pressing a key slowly or typing for longer periods. They also retain a full 4.0mm range of travel, which is less common than I expected among Hall effect gaming keyboards. I can set a very shallow actuation point for movement keys in competitive games without making the entire board feel like a hair trigger. For typing, I prefer a deeper actuation and the full key travel because it feels more natural and gives me fewer accidental inputs. That flexibility makes the Huntsman V3 HE easier to live with as an everyday keyboard rather than something designed exclusively for ranked matches. Rapid trigger works as expected, resetting each key based on movement rather than waiting for it to return to a fixed reset point. In shooters, directional inputs feel crisp and immediate, particularly when rapidly stopping, strafing, or changing direction. Snap Tap can prioritize the newest input between two movement keys, while Snap Flex adds another way to activate commands based on releasing a key. These features will matter most to serious FPS players, but the adjustable actuation is useful even outside competitive gaming. I cannot pretend the jump from an already fast gaming keyboard is transformative in every game, but inputs feel consistently immediate, and there is no sense that the keyboard is holding anything back. It is also possible to store multiple profiles, which is useful when I want aggressive gaming settings without using those same settings while typing or programming. I generally like the 65% layout because it leaves much more space for the mouse while retaining dedicated arrow keys. It is compact enough for an FPS setup without feeling as restrictive as a 60% board, although anyone who regularly uses the function row, navigation cluster, or numpad should expect a period of adjustment. The secondary functions are manageable, but they are still secondary functions. Build quality is appropriately solid for the price. The aluminum top case gives the board a sturdy feel, the doubleshot PBT keycaps have a pleasant texture, and the detachable USB-C cable makes it easier to pack or replace the cable later. The switches sound and feel much more refined than Razer’s earlier analog optical boards, though this is still a gaming keyboard rather than a heavily dampened custom mechanical board. At $120, this is competitively priced for a Hall effect keyboard from a major gaming brand, especially with 8000Hz polling, rapid trigger, adjustable actuation, onboard profiles, and a full 4.0mm travel range. The real improvement for me is not one headline feature but how much better these magnetic switches feel. Overall I'm very happy with my purchase", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 9, 2026"}, {"review_id": "RQL75GJKVLF7Z", "reviewer_name": "Adam Darling", "headline": "Elite Magnetic TKL Keyboard With Precision Control", "review_text": "The Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic Tenkeyless is engineered as a competitive‐grade keyboard built around Hall Effect Magnetic Switches, offering adjustable actuation from 0.1 mm to 4.0 mm and a 100‐million keystroke lifespan (). This switch architecture eliminates debounce delay entirely, enabling instantaneous actuation and reset behavior that mechanical switches simply cannot match. The magnetic sensing provides exceptionally consistent input recognition, and the keyboard’s internal calibration system compensates for magnetic interference to maintain stable performance over time. Combined with the TKL layout, which frees up desk space for low‐sensitivity mouse movement, the Huntsman V3 HE is clearly designed for players who rely on precision micro‐adjustments and rapid directional changes. One of the most defining features is Rapid Trigger, which allows keys to reset the moment they begin to rise rather than waiting for a fixed reset point. This dramatically increases responsiveness in FPS titles, enabling faster counter‐strafes, smoother movement corrections, and more reliable repeated inputs. Esports.gg’s testing highlights how Rapid Trigger transforms WASD control, making movement feel “snappy, predictable, and extremely responsive” — a sentiment that aligns with real‐world gameplay impressions. The keyboard also supports Dynamic Keystroke, allowing up to four actions on a single key at different actuation depths, and Snap Flex, which assigns one action on press and another on release. These features give competitive players granular control over movement, utility activation, and complex keybind setups, especially in games like Valorant, CS2, and Apex Legends (). The Huntsman V3 HE’s 8000 Hz HyperPolling is another major technical advantage. With true 8000 Hz performance, the keyboard sends input data to the PC eight times more frequently than standard 1000 Hz keyboards, reducing average latency to 0.60 ms — roughly 8% faster than competing high‐end boards (). In fast‐paced shooters, this reduction in input delay contributes to more immediate movement and firing responses. Esports.gg’s analysis notes that the keyboard feels “instantaneous,” with no perceptible delay between keypress and on‐screen action. For competitive players who rely on tight timing windows, this level of responsiveness provides a measurable advantage. Build quality is another strong point. The keyboard uses a 5052 aluminum alloy top case, which gives it a rigid, premium feel while keeping weight manageable for LAN events. The switches are factory‐lubricated, and a dense internal foam layer improves acoustics, reducing hollow resonance and delivering a smoother, more muted sound profile. The doubleshot PBT keycaps resist shine and wear, maintaining texture even under heavy daily use. The detachable USB‐C cable and hybrid onboard storage for up to six profiles add practical flexibility, especially for players who switch between systems or travel frequently (). Razer’s software approach is also noteworthy. The Huntsman V3 HE supports Synapse for Web, allowing users to adjust actuation, Rapid Trigger sensitivity, polling rate, lighting, and keybinds directly through a browser without installing software — ideal for tournament environments or shared PCs. The keyboard’s Chroma RGB is bright and evenly diffused, and while lighting is not the focus of this model, it integrates cleanly with competitive setups. Real‐world impressions consistently highlight the keyboard’s stability, predictable actuation behavior, and the immediate improvement in movement control during gameplay. Overall, the Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic Tenkeyless delivers exceptional responsiveness, deep customization, durable construction, and esports‐grade precision. Its combination of Hall Effect Magnetic Switches, Rapid Trigger, Dynamic Keystroke, Snap Tap, and true 8000 Hz HyperPolling makes it one of the most technically advanced competitive keyboards available. For players who prioritize movement accuracy, instant input recognition, and customizable actuation, this keyboard offers a genuine performance advantage that is immediately noticeable in high‐speed FPS environments.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 2, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R38HCBDIW4X7RK", "reviewer_name": "Terrorgod", "headline": "Maybe im ready to give Razer another chance", "review_text": "The Razer Huntsman V3 HE Magnetic Mini keyboard is the latest addition to their Hall Effect Magnetic keyboard lineup. If you haven't been keeping up with keyboard technologies, compared to traditional keyboard switches made by companies like Cherry, they are now utilizing magnets and lasers to create a much more responsive key press reducing latency and allowing for customizable key actuation based on the users preference. I am a hobbyist with keyboard tech, where I have built a good variety of keyboards with DIY kits, customized some of my own, and tend to go out of my way to try new technologies. This is my third time trying a Hall Effect keyboard, with my first being the Steelseries Apex Pro ( with HyperMagnetic switches) and the original Razer Huntsman. I didn't hold onto either of those keyboards very long as at the time they were very expensive compared to their traditional counterparts. They also didn't wow me out of the box with their switch technology. Keypresses felt weak, as if there was no feedback to register that I had hit a key. It also took a lot of tweaking to get them to what I would consider a usable state with accurate typing. Which leaves me with the new Razer Huntsman, where I am happy to report it doesn't share any of these problems. The recent revisions have made many changes, improving the texture on the keycaps, the sound of the keypresses, the out of box actuation is exactly what I want, and the 8khz polling is probably helping with how responsive the keys feel. I generally use full size keyboards as I like to have a numpad, but the feel of this keyboard is winning me over to make it my daily driver away from my Mountain Everest Max with Cherry Blues. Lubed Holy Panda switches are the only ones I own that might feel a little bit better than these, but the overall responsiveness of these HE Magentics is something I haven't had the pleasure of experiencing before. My closing statement will be that I started my PC peripheral journey with Razer back when they released the first Blackwidow keyboard & OG Razer Naga. I have watched their products go through sharp declines, and had a time of regret after recommending them to several friends and watching their mice break down on them within a year each. I am hesitant to recommend them again due to the many issues I have had across a few years before ultimately moving away from their products entirely. I will update this review if I encounter any issues with the keyboard as I daily drive it. Post note: I forgot to mention Synapse in this review, as I don't really want to use it. I will add it in if I change my mind but luckily the keyboard works fine without it. Windows Dynamic Lighting isn't working with the keyboard out of the box but I know of other 3rd party software that used to work with Razer that I preferred. After one pop up the Razer software installer hasn't appeared again which is nice.", "rating": "4.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 3, 2026"}]

reviews: [{"review_id": "R20G26MQ7Q4CRB", "reviewer_name": "Yo_Paisan", "headline": "Never thought I'd love a keyboard so much...", "review_text": "It's taking a little getting used to the slightly different arrangement of some keys but man... overall, this keyboard KICKS TAIL!!! As it turns out there were. Oddly, they didn't work though. The keyboard refused to light up, the keys meant to dim or brighten it doing nothing at all. As I began a search to see if this was a common issue, the backlight finally came on. No idea what changed. Pretty standard white LED backlights. First of all, the build quality is inexcusable for a $150+ keyboard, especially from a brand like Logitech. The space bar and the backspace keys squeak horribly every time I press them. That means that if you aren't constantly typing, the backlight will be turning on and off in a way that is very visually distracting at the bottom of your vision. Furthermore, the caps lock key has a distracting blinking whenever it is on, especially annoying if you are gaming and caps lock is set to something like toggle run/walk. The keyboard is Bluetooth only, which seems to work fine. But I would have liked to have the option to plug it in like a normal USB keyboard. As far as I know the USB plug is only for charging, but also leaves an always illuminated and fairly bright \"charging\" LED, very obnoxious if your computer is in your bedroom. Definitely won't be my last.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on July 17, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R15F8S2EFOVEKI", "reviewer_name": "Daniel C.", "headline": "Beware the USB dongles", "review_text": "Original review: It's a keyboard an it works After hearing people rave about mechanical keyboards, I decided to get myself one. I am not sure how representative of mechanical keyboards this one is, but I find it to be very similar to everything I have used before. The keys don't feel \"clicky\" at all. In fact, I am constantly running into an issue of resting my hands on the keyboard, and \"mushing down\" a key by mistake (in other words, \"wwwwwwwwwwwwwwwww\" because my finger pressed a key without me even noticing). I think I can get used to pulling my hands away from the keyboard to keep that from happening, but I find it weird that I now have to do this. I assumed the keys would be harder to press, not mushier than the cheap-o keyboards I have had. Another issue I have had is that the keyboard is not flat. I have tested it on multiple surfaces, including a glass table. I ended having to prop one side up with some paper. Not too happy about that. For whatever reason, this does not have a print screen key. Luckily you can remap it using the Logi Options+ software. Honestly, at this price, I am not sure I would recommend this keyboard. Ok, so why 4 stars? It does have some positive points. First, it looks pretty sharp. Second, aside from not sitting flat, it feels solid / well-built / quality. It is small, yet it is heavier than most keyboards. I am used to keyboards lasting \"forever\", so I will update here if/when I run into issues. Third, switching between different machines works flawlessly. Fourth, it allows me to bring my settings to all computers (e.g. remapping the screen capture key). Fifth, it has a rechargeable battery and it lasts long enough that I never have to worry. I do have a charging cable right on my desk, so every once in a while I just leave it plugged in, so I have never seen it go below 85%. What else can I say, it is a keyboard and it works. ----- Updated review: beware the USB dongles. Logitech mouses and keyboards (e.g. \"MX Mechanical\", \"MX Master 3s\", \"MX Anywhere 3\") connect either via Bluetooth, or via a USB dongle. However, the USB dongles are not all the same. For example, the \"MX mechanical\" keyboard only connects to a \"bolt\" dongle; and the \"MX Anywhere 3\" mouse only connects to a \"unifying\" dongle. Unfortunately, there is no clear guide / summary for which devices go together. You just have to check each device before buying to see what dongle it uses. Devices in the same generation are *not* guaranteed to use the same type of dongle. Here is my experience: I setup for myself a MX mechanical keyboard + MX Master 3s mouse and everything works fine. Both devices connect to a \"bolt\" dongle, so I have a \"bolt\" dongle on my laptop, and another \"bolt\" dongle on a desktop computer. I can switch between laptop and desktop with a press of a button. The keyboard/mouse itself is fine, the review can be seen above. My wife saw my setup and wanted the same, but she didn't want the MX Master 3s mouse (\"it is too big\"), so I got her a this same \"MX Mechanical\" keyboard and a pink \"MX Anywhere 3\". As it turns out, the mouse does not come with a \"bolt\" dongle, it comes with a \"unifying\" dongle. So now I have one \"bolt\" dongle which connects only to the keyboard, and one \"unifying\" dongle which connects only to the mouse. Thus, to \"fix\" this situation, I either need to use Bluetooth for everything (which I was trying to avoid to begin with), or I need to purchase 1 extra bolt dongle and 1 extra unifying dongle, so that each computer has both a \"unifying\" and a \"bolt\" dongle. Let's hope I have enough USB ports, or I will also need a USB hub. Even if you are aware that different dongles exist, you still need to be careful. If you buy a \"MX Anywhere 3\", you get a \"unifying\" dongle, but if you buy a \"MX Anywhere 3 for business\", then it has a \"bolt\" dongle. This is, by the way, how I ended up with a \"unifying\" dongle - while browsing the products, I opened up two tabs, one with a black MX Anywhere 3, and one with a pink MX Anywhere 3, except one of them was \"for business\" and the other was not. You might think this mess would warrant giant disclaimers (\"DOES NOT HAVE A BOLT CONNECTOR\"), or some kind of guide for which devices go together, but nope. For extra hilarity, Amazon bundles a \"MX mechanical mini\" (bolt) with a \"MX Anywhere 3\" (unifying). The whole thing is confusing, misleading, and just terrible user/customer experience. If I could start over, I would just get something else.", "rating": "3.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on December 23, 2022"}]

It’s a well-built keyboard with some excellent features and clever design choices. The cable is thick, long, and even has a nice touch — the SteelSeries logo on the USB plug. The RGB effects are top-notch, with smooth transitions both on keypress and when idle. I was genuinely excited about all of this... until I noticed what was missing. And for me, that’s a big deal. Let’s break it down.😁 ### What Makes It (Almost) 5 Stars – The Good:😃 - Excellent Media Controls: The volume wheel is fantastic: easy to reach, smooth to use, and includes a click-to-mute function. The menu button also works similarly to the playback controls found on many headsets with built-in microphones or hands-free kits. Super convenient. - Onboard Controls – No Software Needed: You can manage brightness, RGB colors, effects, profiles, and more — all from the keyboard itself. No software required. Only macros can’t be directly viewed or edited in menu, which is a small detail worth noting. - Smart OLED Display: It shows the status of Num Lock, Caps Lock, Scroll Lock, and whether the Windows key is disabled. Very handy (though there’s a small catch — more on that below). - Customization & Visual Feedback: Besides full per-key RGB customization and reactive effects, pressing the “Fn” key (the SteelSeries logo key) lights up related function keys in red for quick reference. It’s super helpful... but again, not perfect (you can’t change the color — more on that too). - Profile Memory Built-In: You can save up to 5 profiles directly on the keyboard and toggle them on/off without cycling through all of them. I personally use just two: one for gaming and one for productivity. ### The Not-So-Good – My Gripes😒: - No Dedicated Context Menu Key: This is my biggest issue. A full-size keyboard should include the dedicated menu key (the \"right-click menu\" key). SteelSeries replaced it with their custom “Fn” key, which really disrupted my usual workflow. I ended up switching to Shift + F10 to keep things consistent across devices. - Fn Key Can’t Be Reassigned: The SteelSeries logo key, which replaces the context menu key, is fixed — it can’t be remapped. Personally, I’d have preferred having the Windows key only on the left, and using the right one for Fn, keeping the menu key in its usual place. - OLED Button Always Lit: The brightness of the button next to the OLED screen cannot be dimmed or turned off. If you’re working in a dark room or watching movies, this little light will keep shining at you — kind of annoying. - OLED Icons Overlap Custom Logos: If you upload a custom image to the OLED screen, the status icons for Num Lock, Caps, etc. may overlap your logo. Not a dealbreaker, but it limits how creative you can get with personalization. - No Visual Feedback When Windows Key Is Locked: Unlike other lock states (like Caps Lock), there’s no lighting change or visual indicator on the keyboard itself when the Windows key is disabled — just a small icon on the OLED. Feels inconsistent. - Function Key Highlight Color Can’t Be Changed: When pressing “Fn,” the related keys light up red — but that red is not customizable. If your RGB theme is red, this effect becomes basically invisible. - Slight Input Delay: There’s a small delay in key activation. I don’t notice it while typing or working, but for competitive gaming, it might matter. Rtings.com confirmed this in their testing too. - Non-Replaceable Hybrid Switches This is the most serious issue. The switches aren’t standard and can’t be replaced by the user. If a key fails, you’re stuck with relying on warranty, support... or scavenging another board. Not great. ### Neutral Points – Might Be Good or Bad Depending on You🤷🏻♂️: - Actuation Distance: I switched from a keyboard with ultra-light 0.8 mm actuation, and I kept typing extra characters. The Apex 5 feels much more precise and helped reduce typos — a big plus for me. - Key Feel & Keycaps: The keycaps aren’t made from premium material, but they feel decent. Coming from linear switches, the tactile feel took a bit of getting used to — but I adjusted quickly. - Magnetic Wrist Rest: I don’t use it much, but the magnets are strong and hold it firmly in place. - Macro Labeling (M1, M2, etc.): Some keys are labeled as macro keys (M1, M2...), which can be confusing at first — but you’ll get used to it. - Customization Without Software: You can change basic RGB effects and profiles directly from the keyboard. The software adds more depth, but it’s nice that you’re not forced to use it. - USB Plug with Logo: A small but smart touch: the SteelSeries logo on the USB plug helps you spot which device you’re plugging in. - No Physical Lock LEDs: The lock indicators (Num Lock, Caps, Scroll) have been moved to the OLED screen, and you can set those keys to change color when active. Some might miss the old-school LED lights, but I’m fine with it. ### Final Verdict 💸😇 The SteelSeries Apex 5 is a well-built, visually polished keyboard with great RGB, useful media controls, and a solid set of features for gamers and professionals alike. It's base functionality of controlling the volume of your computer works like a charm but it's when you get into the submenus that you can really see where it shines. You see, I am someone who bounces between a macbook pro for work and a windows PC for play and so I'm constantly bouncing between the two. Before, I had a mac specific keyboard and a windows specific keyboard, both occupying space on my desk. From there, I can easily use the digital display + volume knob to switch my connection between the two. Heck, if I needed to add another couple I could. Remember the secondary functions of the various keys? If you look on the side of the 'A' and 'S' keys, you can see that they read 'WIN' and 'MAC' respectively. So to switch formats, all you have to do is hit 'Fn' + 'A' or 'S' to switch between the two. This really pushed my like for this keyboard to love. Cons: The only thing I can really think of is a nitpick and is possibly even already a function, I'd just have to read through the manual a bit more. Videos that I watched were a good indicator, but as other reviews have said, they really do not do the keyboard justice for how it actually sounds. The letters themselves are very creamy, while the function buttons (spacebar, shift, enter, backspace, etc.) have a much deeper \"thocky\" sound to them. If you're on the fence, at least try it and return if it's not for you. The functionality is incredible. There are a ton of lighting options that you can play with. I love the the keyboard has both a USB-A and USB-C port. I am a huge advocate for technology having USB-C as an option, as it is much more convenient, provide faster transfer times, and faster charging times. Speaking of charging, the battery life on this keyboard is excellent. I seem to get about a week's worth of charge with extreme use daily. I know that the keyboard is hot swappable, meaning you can swap out the switches, which ultimately determine the sound of the keyboard, but personally, I haven't messed with that, as I love the way it sounds now. Overall, this is an excellent keyboard. If you're in the market for a wireless keyboard that sounds great, this is the best option out there! However, after extensive investigation (because I really wanted to keep this keyboard for its mechanical build), I finally discovered that the issues were caused by an obscure, lingering USB driver from a device no longer connected to my PC. There is a point somewhere along the key travel where pressure slightly decreases, but you’d need to press very slowly and have an extremely sensitive touch to notice it. In actual typing, it feels - at least to me - indistinguishable from a regular linear switch. Omitting those toddler-toy-like features and lowering the price - or populating that space with more keys - would be more useful, in my opinion. I used the included keycap puller to swap the positions of the 'Home' and 'Del' keys, then made the change in the RK software. It took just a few seconds. These settings are retained even if you unplug the keyboard or uninstall the RK software entirely from your PC. All things considered, in terms of mechanical construction, this is a very good keyboard. I do wish the switches were more tactile, but that’s just a matter of personal preference. These switches are still decent, and I’ll probably swap them out in the future for some Kailh clicky switches.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on June 20, 2025"}, {"review_id": "R36MSXQVTXWN9G", "reviewer_name": "Cap'n Stoob", "headline": "Good keyboard but little support for Mac", "review_text": "The keyboard part is awesome and the keys feel good with a satisfying clack that isn't sharp or too loud. Still, the keyboard is worth keeping even if the program needed to control the LED lights and other functions is Windows only.", "rating": "4.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on March 3, 2026"}]

reviews: [{"review_id": "R1DFN4WD4T6ZBS", "reviewer_name": "LDRB", "headline": "Finally found the Fitness Watch that works as advertised!", "review_text": "I have tested numerous “smart watches” in my quest to find a decent replacement for my ever faithful and reliable, Fitbit Versa 4. I purchased it almost four years ago to replace the original Fitbit Versa. But then Google took over Fitbit, and I was looking for a reliable alternative to the Fitbit products. I tried a Samsung Galaxy watch 7 that lost steps by the thousands each day. I tried an Apple Smart Watch that sometimes had to be charged more than once EVERY DAY! I tried a Parsonver (less expensive) but even though it was advertised and labeled IP 68, (indicating that it would withstand submersion in water) I actually received an email from the company before the watch was even delivered advising me to be careful even showering or washing my hands with it on! SERIOUSLY???? And the step counts were not even close to correct! Then I tried an Amazfit BIP6 (also advertised as IP 68, but clearly IS NOT) and thought I had finally found what I was looking for, until it completely malfunctioned after only 3 weeks of use. So Amazon replaced it with ANOTHER BIP6, and that one lasted almost 5 months before it began to seriously malfunction and the touchscreen no longer worked. So my new search began and I decided to give Garmin a try as my walking and swimming buddies swear by their Garmins, and the results that they get with them compare favorably to my old Fitbit. I have now only had the Garmin Vivoactive 5 for about a month, but so far, it is AWESOME! It tracks extremely well with the Fitbit, and I have had no issues whatsoever with water infiltration. If that changes, I will be back to downgrade my rating, but so far, so GREAT! This proves that you don’t have to buy the most expensive models of ANY brand of fitness watch to find one that does what you need it to do. Most of them have more functions than you will ever need or use anyway. I bought separate, different color bands to customize it and love that you have a lot of choices for watch faces, so pick the one that works best for you! (Although - once again, Fitbit has a much better and more user friendly watch face selection portal!) The one potential “glitch” I thought I had finally discovered with my Vivoactive 5, but which turned out not to be an issue, occurred when I was flying internationally. I was returning from Europe to the US on an evening flight where the time in the US was six hours earlier. So both my FITBIT and my Garmin thought that when enough flight time had elapsed, they went past midnight and started their metrics over as a new day - meaning steps completely zeroed out and started over. But not long after I landed at 7 pm US time, my Fitbit picked back up with the previous day’s step tally, but my Garmin still showed the reduced step count tallied as a “new day”. I was disappointed with this until I checked the metrics in the Garmin app and noted that the “two day tallies” indicated on the watch itself were actually (appropriately!) counted and displayed as a single day step counts in the app. So yes, I am sold on the Garmin. But I do still have to wonder why if FITBIT - even early versions - could have successfully addressed ALL of the issues I have found with so many competitor brands, why can’t all the others? Maybe I shouldn’t have been so wary of Google taking over Fitbit when I started investigating other Smart watches, but I learned a lot about different brands and their bogus IP 68 and 5 ATM ratings! So to reiterate, Garmin is exactly what it says it is, and Fitbit is as well. Do your comparisons!", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 1, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R3NQ6GTCJGRL6M", "reviewer_name": "Kim", "headline": "Love me a Garmin", "review_text": "I've been using Garmin for running for years now. They've improved a lot! This one does everything I need and more. I like the body battery, sleep info. The 5 syncs up to GPS much faster than my 4 to run or walk. I love the music, however, my headphones sometimes disconnect to the watch while running. Not sure if it's the headphones or the watch. It's pretty easy to use if you've had one before. It has changed on the strength where you hit the bottom button vs tapping the watch to enter weight/reps (don't have to do that anymore, not that it was a problem). Overall I'm super satisfied. Can see it better as well with the new display.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 19, 2026"}, {"review_id": "ROY0X1HZZ886K", "reviewer_name": "Jared King", "headline": "The best fitness tracker I've used", "review_text": "I'm coming from an Apple Watch Series 5. I had gotten frustrated with the battery life and sleep tracking and wanted to see if a more fitness-focused watch would be a better fit. I'm not a big runner or someone who does a lot of intense exercise, but I do like to track my exercise and sleep and get nudges to move when I've been sitting down for too long. I also like to get notifications on my wrist without needing to pull out my phone. Compared to the Apple Watch, the first major thing I noticed was this is nowhere close in terms of smarts. I had gotten used to Apple's smooth interface, built in microphone and speaker for voice commands, and often useful apps that can be used without needing to get my phone out. That being said, after a few days I can confidently say that I don't need them. I would argue that Garmin knows what this is and what it is not - it's a fitness device first and foremost, and everything else comes second. And on that basis they nailed it - the fitness tracking has been excellent and noticeably better than the Apple Watch especially in sleep tracking. I also much prefer their approach to goals, which tracks exercise over the course of a week rather than focusing specifically on individual days. Whenever I was sick or had a down day I would feel guilty if I didn't close all of my rings on my Apple Watch, but I don't feel that same pressure with the Garmin. I do miss being able to use voice commands with my watch, but I could have gotten a more expensive Garmin if I really wanted that, and I don't think it's worth it for me. The second thing I noticed: not having to charge your watch every day is a game changer. This was easily my biggest frustration with the Apple Watch since it's marketed as a device you wear 24x7 and yet needs to be charged every day. And considering how long it took to charge my Series 5, this was a major annoyance. I couldn't charge it overnight, because I wanted sleep tracking. I couldn't charge it in the morning, because I like to start off my day with exercise and it doesn't charge fast enough to do it after a workout and before work. And if I charged it in the evening, I would often forget to put it on before bed and miss out on the sleep tracking. The Garmin is a breath of fresh air by comparison - I charge it about once a week, and with my relatively light usage it can probably go close to two. I took a multi day trip recently and I didn't once have to worry about charging my watch, which was a pleasant change. Overall I think this watch is a great fit for a more casual user who isn't running marathons but wants to track fitness and sleep and get some extras like smartphone notifications and see the weather at a glance. If you want something with more smart features and better build quality (i.e. more metal and less plastic), then the Venu might be a better fit. Or they have the Forerunner if you do run marathons. Or a bunch of other models for more specific use cases. But I would highly recommend giving this watch a try if you're looking for the same things that I am.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 17, 2024"}, {"review_id": "R6H93OO3CVD5L", "reviewer_name": "KW", "headline": "Great choice for my sensitive skin.", "review_text": "Great so far. I tried another brand the caused a rash from the heart rate monitor (not the band because I swap them for cloth or leather). Garmin Vivoactive 5 has not caused any skin irritation! I am pleased with the metrics it gives. The app takes some getting used to, but it isn't complicated to navigate...just different from fitbit. So far the battery charge lasts for at least 7 days. It charges quickly. I like the screen size, metrics and words are easy to read. The screen reacts well to touch even with a screen protector on. It is easy to access the watches features. I like the wake up summary. It gives me prompts to move and stretch. It gives sleep advice and measures body battery throughout the day. The watch is comfortable to wear and looks great with everything. I swap between a nylon band and leather band. I would highly recommend.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on May 22, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R13N6UKBCYYZ4A", "reviewer_name": "Omega Man", "headline": "I love this thing. Not the least expensive, but probably the best bang for the buck.", "review_text": "I’m someone who really really did not want a watch of any sort, especially not an Apple Watch or anything else that is bloated with unnecessary hardware that needs to be charged every single day. Charging a phone every day is enough of a pain without needing to add any other junk, so no thanks to the useless gimmick-loaded “smart” watches. But I really needed to do fitness tracking because without some sort of gadget I just have zero idea how lazy or not lazy I’ve been lately and whether or not I need to get at least some minimal exercise. And my #1 must have feature is week-long battery charge life. This watch is good enough, even though the battery life might be more like 5 days in some cases if you’re using it for activities a lot where the gps is turned on. But for those not running with the gps every day or constantly tinkering with it a full battery charge seems to last a week. That is, charge it for an hour on Sunday and no need to charge it again until the same time next Sunday. You could get the battery to last longer if you’re willing to shut off absolutely everything that might use more power. I started out with a Garmin vivosmart 5 because I didn’t think I needed anything beyond that, but I have sleep problems and decided I needed better sleep tracking. So I ended up with this one even though I don’t really care about random silly “apps” on a watch. Overall this watch has been excellent. It has a very good UI and the fitness tracking features a quite good. The sleep tracking is decent, but still has its issues that hopefully Garmin will fix with software updates. In particular the “nap tracking” doesn’t seem fully baked yet, and things like laying back in a recliner reading a book or watching TV can get falsely detected as a “nap”. Then there’s no way to delete a false nap on the watch or in the Garmin Connect app. There are still a few minor bugs that some people will run into but they seem to be things that can be fixed with firmware updates and I haven’t run into anything completely feature-breaking. If you feel like messing with it you can also install some “apps” like custom watch face designs or sunset/sunrise times, more detailed weather and such. But even without installing anything the watch does everything needed for health and fitness stuff. Almost all of the apps that come with the device can be uninstalled, so if you don’t need “women’s health tracking” for example then you can just remove that to free up space. Their mobile app is pretty well designed and only awkward in some parts of the configuration. The watch reliably synchronizes as long as you leave the phone app running in the background and I’ve never had any Bluetooth connection failures, lag, or lost pairings. Things that the watch is not good for are things that you’d typically use a phone for like communication, turn by turn navigation, maps, games, and such. But I don’t want a watch to do any of that stuff and I’d rather have it save its battery charge so I don’t have to charge it constantly. So overall, this is “the” watch you want if you want as little nonsense as possible and don’t want to worry about battery charge all the time but still need full health and fitness tracking stuff beyond what the $75-150 models offer. And there are also no subscriptions required.", "rating": "4.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on March 11, 2024"}, {"review_id": "RLIHT6VF7W7Q", "reviewer_name": "Connie D", "headline": "It's a keeper!", "review_text": "I was concerned the watch face would be too big but I got used to it right away. The size makes the display easy to read so I can keep track of my steps with just a glance. I also use the bike riding function (GPS) to track miles. I wish it would convert miles biked to steps taken but not sure any watch does that. I used the golf app the other day for distance and scoring. With any new electronics it takes a while and patience to figure it out but once I did I really like it. I'm still learning. I also like the sleep tracking function. Long battery life.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 2, 2026"}, {"review_id": "RR5MJPNZSAFNR", "reviewer_name": "Cornelia", "headline": "Garmin vívoactive® 5 Health & Fitness GPS Smartwatch", "review_text": "The Garmin vívoactive® 5 has been a great watch to help monitor my daily activities, sleep, heart rate, and so much more. I wasn't so interested in the idea of connecting to my phone but rather the health benefits. It was a great purchase. The screen size is not too large for my small 5 inch wrist, but also large enough that I can clearly see the screen. The watch was easy to set up, make adjustments to as I learn about the various functions, and was easy to connect to my phone and work benefits. I like that I am able to select which features I would like to use. Garmin is very compatible with many fitness programs. I don't have good success wearing a silicone strap so I did purchase other bands which were simple to remove and connect to the watch head. I believe Garmin was a very good choice for a first health and fitness watch for me.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 8, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R2IAH62P64EBO5", "reviewer_name": "A", "headline": "Nice watch, has some flaws", "review_text": "Just received the watch today, it’s nice but I have some concerns. For starters the band is completely silicone and plastic- the buckle piece is plastic, even the case around the watch is plastic. For $200 you’d think it would at-least be metal. The setup was easy- but came with very little instruction for other things like changing watch faces, setting up apps, etc. Learning how to use the watch and what the buttons all do is pure guessing. The charger is USB-C- if it wasn’t for my laptop I would have no way to charge the watch. Should have come with a compatible block. UPDATE: After using the watch for several days I do like it. While the overall construction (plastic casing) could be better, the overall operation works great. Steps and heart rate seem accurate. The display looks nice, customizable, and the watch is comfortable. The stress levels don’t seem to be accurate. I get “high stress” alerts when all I’ve been doing is laying in bed all day. Just add a titanium casing to the surrounding of the watch and provide more thorough instructions on overall use + updates for accuracy on certain apps and it would be perfect!", "rating": "4.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on January 20, 2026"}]

reviews: [{"review_id": "R1DFN4WD4T6ZBS", "reviewer_name": "LDRB", "headline": "Finally found the Fitness Watch that works as advertised!", "review_text": "I have tested numerous “smart watches” in my quest to find a decent replacement for my ever faithful and reliable, Fitbit Versa 4. I purchased it almost four years ago to replace the original Fitbit Versa. But then Google took over Fitbit, and I was looking for a reliable alternative to the Fitbit products. I tried a Samsung Galaxy watch 7 that lost steps by the thousands each day. I tried an Apple Smart Watch that sometimes had to be charged more than once EVERY DAY! I tried a Parsonver (less expensive) but even though it was advertised and labeled IP 68, (indicating that it would withstand submersion in water) I actually received an email from the company before the watch was even delivered advising me to be careful even showering or washing my hands with it on! SERIOUSLY???? And the step counts were not even close to correct! Then I tried an Amazfit BIP6 (also advertised as IP 68, but clearly IS NOT) and thought I had finally found what I was looking for, until it completely malfunctioned after only 3 weeks of use. So Amazon replaced it with ANOTHER BIP6, and that one lasted almost 5 months before it began to seriously malfunction and the touchscreen no longer worked. So my new search began and I decided to give Garmin a try as my walking and swimming buddies swear by their Garmins, and the results that they get with them compare favorably to my old Fitbit. I have now only had the Garmin Vivoactive 5 for about a month, but so far, it is AWESOME! It tracks extremely well with the Fitbit, and I have had no issues whatsoever with water infiltration. If that changes, I will be back to downgrade my rating, but so far, so GREAT! This proves that you don’t have to buy the most expensive models of ANY brand of fitness watch to find one that does what you need it to do. Most of them have more functions than you will ever need or use anyway. I bought separate, different color bands to customize it and love that you have a lot of choices for watch faces, so pick the one that works best for you! (Although - once again, Fitbit has a much better and more user friendly watch face selection portal!) The one potential “glitch” I thought I had finally discovered with my Vivoactive 5, but which turned out not to be an issue, occurred when I was flying internationally. I was returning from Europe to the US on an evening flight where the time in the US was six hours earlier. So both my FITBIT and my Garmin thought that when enough flight time had elapsed, they went past midnight and started their metrics over as a new day - meaning steps completely zeroed out and started over. But not long after I landed at 7 pm US time, my Fitbit picked back up with the previous day’s step tally, but my Garmin still showed the reduced step count tallied as a “new day”. I was disappointed with this until I checked the metrics in the Garmin app and noted that the “two day tallies” indicated on the watch itself were actually (appropriately!) counted and displayed as a single day step counts in the app. So yes, I am sold on the Garmin. But I do still have to wonder why if FITBIT - even early versions - could have successfully addressed ALL of the issues I have found with so many competitor brands, why can’t all the others? Maybe I shouldn’t have been so wary of Google taking over Fitbit when I started investigating other Smart watches, but I learned a lot about different brands and their bogus IP 68 and 5 ATM ratings! So to reiterate, Garmin is exactly what it says it is, and Fitbit is as well. Do your comparisons!", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 1, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R3NQ6GTCJGRL6M", "reviewer_name": "Kim", "headline": "Love me a Garmin", "review_text": "I've been using Garmin for running for years now. They've improved a lot! This one does everything I need and more. I like the body battery, sleep info. The 5 syncs up to GPS much faster than my 4 to run or walk. I love the music, however, my headphones sometimes disconnect to the watch while running. Not sure if it's the headphones or the watch. It's pretty easy to use if you've had one before. It has changed on the strength where you hit the bottom button vs tapping the watch to enter weight/reps (don't have to do that anymore, not that it was a problem). Overall I'm super satisfied. Can see it better as well with the new display.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 19, 2026"}, {"review_id": "ROY0X1HZZ886K", "reviewer_name": "Jared King", "headline": "The best fitness tracker I've used", "review_text": "I'm coming from an Apple Watch Series 5. I had gotten frustrated with the battery life and sleep tracking and wanted to see if a more fitness-focused watch would be a better fit. I'm not a big runner or someone who does a lot of intense exercise, but I do like to track my exercise and sleep and get nudges to move when I've been sitting down for too long. I also like to get notifications on my wrist without needing to pull out my phone. Compared to the Apple Watch, the first major thing I noticed was this is nowhere close in terms of smarts. I had gotten used to Apple's smooth interface, built in microphone and speaker for voice commands, and often useful apps that can be used without needing to get my phone out. That being said, after a few days I can confidently say that I don't need them. I would argue that Garmin knows what this is and what it is not - it's a fitness device first and foremost, and everything else comes second. And on that basis they nailed it - the fitness tracking has been excellent and noticeably better than the Apple Watch especially in sleep tracking. I also much prefer their approach to goals, which tracks exercise over the course of a week rather than focusing specifically on individual days. Whenever I was sick or had a down day I would feel guilty if I didn't close all of my rings on my Apple Watch, but I don't feel that same pressure with the Garmin. I do miss being able to use voice commands with my watch, but I could have gotten a more expensive Garmin if I really wanted that, and I don't think it's worth it for me. The second thing I noticed: not having to charge your watch every day is a game changer. This was easily my biggest frustration with the Apple Watch since it's marketed as a device you wear 24x7 and yet needs to be charged every day. And considering how long it took to charge my Series 5, this was a major annoyance. I couldn't charge it overnight, because I wanted sleep tracking. I couldn't charge it in the morning, because I like to start off my day with exercise and it doesn't charge fast enough to do it after a workout and before work. And if I charged it in the evening, I would often forget to put it on before bed and miss out on the sleep tracking. The Garmin is a breath of fresh air by comparison - I charge it about once a week, and with my relatively light usage it can probably go close to two. I took a multi day trip recently and I didn't once have to worry about charging my watch, which was a pleasant change. Overall I think this watch is a great fit for a more casual user who isn't running marathons but wants to track fitness and sleep and get some extras like smartphone notifications and see the weather at a glance. If you want something with more smart features and better build quality (i.e. more metal and less plastic), then the Venu might be a better fit. Or they have the Forerunner if you do run marathons. Or a bunch of other models for more specific use cases. But I would highly recommend giving this watch a try if you're looking for the same things that I am.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 17, 2024"}, {"review_id": "R6H93OO3CVD5L", "reviewer_name": "KW", "headline": "Great choice for my sensitive skin.", "review_text": "Great so far. I tried another brand the caused a rash from the heart rate monitor (not the band because I swap them for cloth or leather). Garmin Vivoactive 5 has not caused any skin irritation! I am pleased with the metrics it gives. The app takes some getting used to, but it isn't complicated to navigate...just different from fitbit. So far the battery charge lasts for at least 7 days. It charges quickly. I like the screen size, metrics and words are easy to read. The screen reacts well to touch even with a screen protector on. It is easy to access the watches features. I like the wake up summary. It gives me prompts to move and stretch. It gives sleep advice and measures body battery throughout the day. The watch is comfortable to wear and looks great with everything. I swap between a nylon band and leather band. I would highly recommend.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on May 22, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R13N6UKBCYYZ4A", "reviewer_name": "Omega Man", "headline": "I love this thing. Not the least expensive, but probably the best bang for the buck.", "review_text": "I’m someone who really really did not want a watch of any sort, especially not an Apple Watch or anything else that is bloated with unnecessary hardware that needs to be charged every single day. Charging a phone every day is enough of a pain without needing to add any other junk, so no thanks to the useless gimmick-loaded “smart” watches. But I really needed to do fitness tracking because without some sort of gadget I just have zero idea how lazy or not lazy I’ve been lately and whether or not I need to get at least some minimal exercise. And my #1 must have feature is week-long battery charge life. This watch is good enough, even though the battery life might be more like 5 days in some cases if you’re using it for activities a lot where the gps is turned on. But for those not running with the gps every day or constantly tinkering with it a full battery charge seems to last a week. That is, charge it for an hour on Sunday and no need to charge it again until the same time next Sunday. You could get the battery to last longer if you’re willing to shut off absolutely everything that might use more power. I started out with a Garmin vivosmart 5 because I didn’t think I needed anything beyond that, but I have sleep problems and decided I needed better sleep tracking. So I ended up with this one even though I don’t really care about random silly “apps” on a watch. Overall this watch has been excellent. It has a very good UI and the fitness tracking features a quite good. The sleep tracking is decent, but still has its issues that hopefully Garmin will fix with software updates. In particular the “nap tracking” doesn’t seem fully baked yet, and things like laying back in a recliner reading a book or watching TV can get falsely detected as a “nap”. Then there’s no way to delete a false nap on the watch or in the Garmin Connect app. There are still a few minor bugs that some people will run into but they seem to be things that can be fixed with firmware updates and I haven’t run into anything completely feature-breaking. If you feel like messing with it you can also install some “apps” like custom watch face designs or sunset/sunrise times, more detailed weather and such. But even without installing anything the watch does everything needed for health and fitness stuff. Almost all of the apps that come with the device can be uninstalled, so if you don’t need “women’s health tracking” for example then you can just remove that to free up space. Their mobile app is pretty well designed and only awkward in some parts of the configuration. The watch reliably synchronizes as long as you leave the phone app running in the background and I’ve never had any Bluetooth connection failures, lag, or lost pairings. Things that the watch is not good for are things that you’d typically use a phone for like communication, turn by turn navigation, maps, games, and such. But I don’t want a watch to do any of that stuff and I’d rather have it save its battery charge so I don’t have to charge it constantly. So overall, this is “the” watch you want if you want as little nonsense as possible and don’t want to worry about battery charge all the time but still need full health and fitness tracking stuff beyond what the $75-150 models offer. And there are also no subscriptions required.", "rating": "4.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on March 11, 2024"}, {"review_id": "RLIHT6VF7W7Q", "reviewer_name": "Connie D", "headline": "It's a keeper!", "review_text": "I was concerned the watch face would be too big but I got used to it right away. The size makes the display easy to read so I can keep track of my steps with just a glance. I also use the bike riding function (GPS) to track miles. Long battery life.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 2, 2026"}, {"review_id": "RR5MJPNZSAFNR", "reviewer_name": "Cornelia", "headline": "Garmin vívoactive® 5 Health & Fitness GPS Smartwatch", "review_text": "The Garmin vívoactive® 5 has been a great watch to help monitor my daily activities, sleep, heart rate, and so much more. I don't have good success wearing a silicone strap so I did purchase other bands which were simple to remove and connect to the watch head. I believe Garmin was a very good choice for a first health and fitness watch for me.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on August 8, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R2IAH62P64EBO5", "reviewer_name": "A", "headline": "Nice watch, has some flaws", "review_text": "Just received the watch today, it’s nice but I have some concerns. The screen is sharp, crisp, gorgeous color and easy to read. I am fairly tech savvy and after a lot of frustration, I could only solve my issues this way. (The companion app was no help.) The biggest problem was the watch would compete with my ear buds, phone or bedside speaker to take over Bluetooth control, and attempt to direct the audio to the watch. Audio would cut in and out as it repeatedly tried to take control. I finally figured out what was wrong when I realized a phone call I received was switched to my watch. I had a Dick Tracy watch! 😂 Lol and the audio is not nearly loud enough to make calls on our listen to music. Overall the watch with its phone app is exceptional to monitor steps, heart rate, sleep patterns, exercise sessions, stress level, water intake, weather and control your phone's music app, camera and much more. It does not measure blood pressure as some reviews suggest. It will connect to your AI asst but I don't need that. I do wish for a way to enter water intake in the watch but for now that has to be done on the phone app. It charges fast and is easy to hook up. The battery lasts about a week but you're mileage may vary depending on your settings. I would definitely recommend buying if you are looking for an easy to read screen that is a giant step up from something like a Fitbit. If you want to send messages or emails, respond to them, see images attached in same then look to spend 5-10 times the price. Me? I'm happy with the purchase. I don't need to make calls on a watch or compose replies to texts and emails on my wrist. I really hope they solve the problem competing for Bluetooth as I'd like to turn on some of the features I had to give up to solve the problem.", "rating": "5.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on March 22, 2026"}, {"review_id": "R2ZZCQQERHAUM8", "reviewer_name": "Kassandra", "headline": "Can't complain...much", "review_text": "Hello there, future watch owners. If you're like me, you've spent wayyy too much time agonizing over which knockoff smart watch to buy, and have probably read every review ever written. So, here is a list of every observed helpful and unfortunate aspect of this quality timepiece. I've been using it about a month. Pros: It looks nice. The screen is large enough to read and navigate easily, without feeling like you have a tablet on your wrist. The responsiveness is decent and the picture is clear. The swipe-right shortcut saves your most recent selections. There are lots of options for what it can do. Workouts, music, phone, calculator, stress, sleep, O2, heart rate, water intake, and something I found especially helpful as someone who leaves their phone lying around, Find My Phone. I've used most of these but have barely scratched the surface on the sports/workouts. Notifications show up with a red dot rather than a large icon, which I like and are easy to read and clear. I really like being able to adjust the brightness on the screen, and having a shortcut for the wake gesture; it's easy to turn off at night - because it's bright enough to burn your retnas - and back on during the day. The flashlight function is very helpful and almost absurdly bright. The alarm works well. The battery has been fantastic. I probably have less notifications set up for social media and email than some, but it easily lasts me a week+, which is way more than my poor, retired 4 year old Versa Lite ever did. Cons: The app sucks. It's like they tracked daily notifications with \"app unpaired from device\" and forgot to fix it. I am re-pairing every couple of days. It links up quickly but I wish it would stay linked. There are no screen protectors available that I've found and as a result, there is already a scratch on the face. There is also a chip off the wrist sensor already, which makes me wonder about the longevity, and my skins safety. I wish that when you pressed the side button from a selection, it would take you back to the menu, rather than back to the home screen, but that's minor. I also haven't found replacement bands. I don't care for the cloth band but I like the silicone. Eventually it will wear out and I would like to be able to replace it. I haven't braved the water with it yet because I'm afraid of drowning it, so I can't speak to that. I think that for the price-point, it is worth it. I threw the extended warranty on it, so I'm basically covered for three years if something messes up and then I just get a new one. Rant over, enjoy your day 🙂 hope it helps!", "rating": "4.0 out of 5 stars", "review_date": "Reviewed in the United States on May 27, 2026"}]

It cost about 3x the amount for the Charge 6 compared to the Fit 3. That's ridiculous. In a head to head comparsion of measurements this is what I see. Fitbit Charge is often slower to start your step counts and the Fit 3 is quicker on that. So you steps counts are going to go up and perhaps the Fit 3 does count some arm motions as steps when it should not. But the Fit 3 is still very close (within 1-3%) with the Charge 6.
